#6356. The 6 Best Metal Detectors for Treasure Hunters and Experts Alike

Find treasure on the beach (or at least a bunch of beer cans) with these top-of-the-line devices.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

You've probably seen a metal detectorist hard at work at a beach or park with their funky-looking gadget and thought, "I wish I had one of those." It's easy to fantasize about stumbling upon a hoard of buried pirate gold or, more realistically, a lost piece of jewelry, but the reality of metal detecting is this: It's more about the process of searching than the actual find itself.

That said, metal detecting can be a fun and relaxing hobby for anyone to try, especially with friends, and the barrier to entry is low. It’s an activity that gives you an excuse to spend a few hours outside, scouring the sand or dirt for coins or who-knows-what, and you might even find something that really makes it worth your while, though it's best if you don't expect to.

To determine the best metal detectors for newbies and experts alike, I tested a number of different models on the beaches and in the parks of South Florida, rating their performance, handling, and overall usability across several different terrains. I also consulted with an expert detectorist who helped me understand what factors to consider when making my choices. No matter which of these machines works best for your use case, all of them are great gets.

I selected the best metal detectors after trying a handful of options that came recommended to me by Jeff Lubbert, an expert detectorist who has been tracking down treasures and finding lost rings since the mid-1980s, and a handful of other expert detectorists.

Lubbert has used his metal detector in 28 states, one United States territory, five foreign countries, and three foreign territories, where he has recovered items adding up to approximately $980,000. He is president of the Eureka Treasure Hunters Club in Denver, Colorado, and has written articles about metal detectors for outlets like American Diggers. He's also appeared on the TV show Forensic Files.

To test accuracy, I buried an old spoon and two different coins—a quarter and a penny—8 inches underground to check their level of discrimination and pinpointing. I also used each detector for several hours in a variety of conditions, including in a grassy park and at the beach, in both dry sand and wet sand, and under several inches of surf.

The Minelab Vanquish 560 is a dynamic metal detector that works well on every terrain, including wet sand, and is incredibly intuitive to use. Unlike the slightly cheaper Vanquish 440, my previous top recommendation, the 560 is waterproof to 16 feet, which makes it suitable for wading and underwater use. It also includes a rechargeable battery, a flashlight, and Bluetooth headphone support, making it one of the most fully-featured detectors in this guide, and especially for this price.

While it only has four find modes (including an adjustable “custom” option). That’s are far fewer than you will find on professional-grade detectors like the Minelab Equinox 900, but it's still much more than enough for most amateur metal detectorists.

The Vanquish 560 punches well above its weight, and value-wise, it's the best detector we tested on a per-dollar basis. It may feel like a splurge for first-timers, but you’re getting what you pay for. And it’s an incredibly handsome upgrade for folks looking strong accuracy and some quality-of-life improvements.

Since I primarily spoke with experts and enthusiasts, the Nokta FindX Pro was not remotely on my radar when I first began my research. But it may just be the best option for new detectorists looking to dip a toe into the hobbyist pool. It’s an all-in-one kit, complete with an effective digging tool, a nice duffel bag, and decent headphones—all for less than $200.

While it is not as accurate as my other recommendations, it’s a more than capable VLF detector. I was able to find items at both parks and beaches, though I noticed that its performance really suffered on wet sand and underwater. Its compact frame and adjustable handle make it accommodating to a wider-than-average range of newcomers, including kids and adults.

If you’re interested in the hobby and don’t want to spend too much to try it, the FindX Pro is a great fit for beginners.

While I wasn’t able to get this detector in for my current round of tests, Lubbert recommended the Minelab Manticore for expert detectorists who want the ultimate metal detector experience. He says it can visualize the ground beneath it in a 2D map, directing you to finds with depths and ID targets. It should work well in any terrain, including underwater, and has the most advanced backlight of any Minelab machine. Plus, with 10 search modes, there are many options for veteran detectorists looking to optimize for a specific type of search.

The price is substantial, but if you’re willing to spend this much money on a detector, I’m confident that it will be worth it.

The Simplex line is often recommended by experts as a good entry point for new detectorists. Nokta is one of the two biggest brands in the metal detecting game—the other is Minelab—and the Simplex Lite is a strong, basic VLF detector. I found it had top-notch discrimination, plenty of find modes, and a good coil size that easily found my testing materials and led me to beer cans, aluminum foil, and plenty of other objects on the beach.

Because this is a single-frequency VLF detector, it doesn’t perform as well as the Vanquish 440, especially on the mineralized sand at saltwater beaches. It’s still a very capable machine, though—even more so if you’re searching for a specific type of item, particularly coins and jewelry. Though it offers fewer customization options than its more expensive multi-frequency counterparts, it’s also much easier to pick up and use as a newcomer.

For those who are looking to spend a bit more, you can upgrade to the Simplex Ultra, which adds Bluetooth support and gives you precision detector tools like target ID scale and depth.

Underwater metal detecting is typically the domain of serious enthusiasts, especially if it’s in seawater. If this sounds intriguing, two different experts for metal detector recommendations (including Lubbert) suggest the XP Deus II, a high-end machine that specializes in just that. Expert Stanley Ross, known as the Metal Detector Man, who we spoke with for this article previously, says that he uses his Deus II to search for lost rings and other jewelry on the beach all the time.

The Deus II has something called "fast multi-frequency" technology, which allows for superior multi-frequency detection in a variety of conditions, and it's rated for up to 20 meters of water, a massive upgrade compared to our other picks that top out at 5 meters of water resistance. Our other multi-frequency picks use similar technology, but the Deus II offers better and faster response in saltwater conditions, making it easier to pinpoint buried targets without having to pass over the same spot multiple times, especially underwater.In order to use the Deus II underwater, however, you'll need a few accessories, including its waterproof wireless headphones and an underwater remote control. While these upgrades are technically “optional” in the sense that you can easily use the Deus II on land without them, they are virtually required for anything beyond getting your ankles wet.

Both of these additions will increase the price of the overall package considerably, depending on which exact model of headphones you choose. Both the $280 WS6 headphones (which can control the detector, but are not recommended for underwater use) and the $749 remote control have slightly different interfaces, but the remote control is generally recommended for both ease of use and underwater functionality. Because of its high customizability and 12 preset modes, the Deus II isn't quite as beginner-friendly as some of our other picks.

While I haven't yet tested the Deus II for myself, it’s highly regarded among enthusiasts. If you're interested in underwater detecting—whether that's wading around or even diving down—this choice will not disappoint.

The Minelab Equinox 900 is the most feature-rich metal detector I tested. From the second I picked it up, I could tell that it would be a cut above the rest. The build quality is noticeably better than that of other, less expensive models I tested—it just feels more substantial.

Its features and performance back up that first impression. The Equinox 900 consistently performed better than its less expensive counterparts as well, pinpointing targets precisely and identifying both their depth and target ID. Though I was able to find my planted targets with every detector, the Equinox 900 directed me precisely to all three, making the process quicker and easier in both dry and wet sand.

It also features a number of settings and tools that improve the detecting experience, including six customizable frequency settings, an easy-adjust handle, and Bluetooth support so you can use wireless headphones. All that customization is incredible if you’re an expert. I personally had more success using the premade settings, but I can see detectorists like Lubbert fine-tuning searches to great effect.

I was especially taken with its handgrip vibration feature, which gives you a rumbling haptic response when the Equinox picks up a target. It’s a great way to get your attention in a loud area, if you’re hearing-impaired, or if you’re just on a long walk and not paying close attention. Personally, I found it very helpful while roaming some very popular stretches of Miami’s beaches.

It’s worth noting that Minelab lists the Equinox 900 as a bit heavier than the other models we tested, though I personally didn’t notice a difference, even after several hours of sweeping. At more than triple the price of my best overall pick, it’s fair to say that the Equinox 900 is an investment for serious hobbyists. But it is far and away the most effective choice I tested and a worthy upgrade.

In addition to a decent pair of headphones, it helps to carry a pinpointer when using your metal detector. These precise, short-range auxiliary detectors assist you with determining the exact location of a find after picking something up with your detector’s large coil.

This one, from Minelab, is relatively expensive, but fully waterproof with five sensitivity levels, and it works very well. It also features ferrous discrimination, which allows it to tell if a target is made of ferrous metals like iron or non-ferrous metals like gold, silver, or copper. It isn’t strictly necessary but is an extra feature you’ll enjoy using in trash-filled parks.

We tested and loved the Minelab Vanquish 440, a slightly cheaper version of our current best overall pick, the Vanquish 560. It was recently replaced with a new and improved model, the Minelab Vanquish 460, which is also a strong choice. We ultimately chose to recommend the 560 because it offers a more robust set of features and works well over more types of terrain.

While shopping for a metal detector, you need to take into account a number of key factors, particularly the type, coil size, weight, and extra features like backlight and frequency customization. Weight and build quality also make a big difference, especially when you use these devices for hours at a time. It was initially hard to weigh these distinct traits, but after testing these machines myself, the features worth springing for became clear.

If you’re going to shop for a hobby-grade metal detector, it’s important to understand how they work. This is fairly technical equipment, so manufacturers will cater their products primarily to veterans who already have a bit of knowledge, which may be intimidating to new people.

Most metal detectors have a round head called the “search coil,” which is the actual detector itself. It has two parts, the transmitter coil and the receiver coil, which work in tandem to produce an electromagnetic field that shoots down into the ground wherever you wave it. When the field hits metal, it triggers another magnetic effect in response, which the coil picks up. Depending on the device, that signal may be able to tell you how deep an object is buried, based on the strength of the response.

Most of the detectors I recommend can determine what kind of metal they’re reading by measuring the object’s “phase shift,” or the time it takes for the object to react when the coil changes its magnetic current. This function, called “discrimination,” can sometimes help you figure out if your quarry is worth digging up before you go to the trouble of getting your digging tools out. However, as Lubbert notes, discrimination is not always reliable, and it’s generally best to err on the side of digging if you think you’ve found something worthwhile.

The first thing to look at before buying a metal detector is where you plan to use it, as some detectors are better equipped to scan specific types of terrain. For example, if you live near the coast and plan to sweep your local beach, you may want a different model than someone looking under hard soil in local parks. Though there are many kinds of detectors, I focused on the two most frequently used by novices and veteran hobbyists.

The physical size of the metal detector coil is important, too. If you don’t sweep the coil over an object, you aren’t going to get a ping, so bigger is better. Under most conditions, Lubbert recommends looking for a coil that’s at least 11 inches in diameter.

That said, Lubbert advises that smaller coils have their uses, especially in wooded areas, since it’s easier to get between twigs, grass, and weeds with a more compact head. Larger coils can theoretically detect objects that are deeper underground, but they’re also more susceptible to electromagnetic interference from the environment. He recommends having both a compact coil and a large coil option if you plan to scan a wide range of environments.

In general, all of my recommendations here seem relatively light on paper—the heaviest weighs only a few pounds. Keep in mind, though, that you could be waving this device around with one arm for hours at a time. Even a few ounces can greatly impact how quickly you tire out.

Mid-range and high-end metal detectors tend to feature backlit displays, which come in handy when searching in low-light conditions. (Some high-end models even come with flashlight functions). Though not a universal feature, I consider this essential for all but the cheapest options.

High-end metal detectors grant you a degree of customization through advanced settings, allowing you to set a specific level of discrimination that, when properly used, can help you identify relics and coins in a variety of environments. You need to know what you’re doing to take full advantage of these do-it-yourself search modes, but there are guides online to help you learn as you go.

Lastly, most metal detectors I researched and/or tested feature built-in batteries that last for hours on a full charge. That said, some models—including one of my picks—use disposable batteries instead. There are advantages and disadvantages to both: Disposable batteries can be replaced quickly, but you need to keep spare cells on you. It comes down to your preference, so go with what feels right.

“Make each swing of the detector take about 2 seconds and overlap your swings so that the coil covers all of the ground,” Lubbert says. “Wear headphones, as it helps you hear those deep target whispers.”

Lubbert also said that detectorists should be happy with what they find, and that you should expect 95 percent of your digs to result in trash. When that happens, be cool, and make sure to dispose of it properly.

According to Lubbert, a dedicated detectorist should have a pinpointer, proper recovery tools like a shovel, and a pouch to store trash and treasure separately.

Based on my testing experience and to echo his point above, I found headphones to be a must-have when using a metal detector, as the built-in speakers are difficult to hear, especially on a crowded beach.

Finding a legal place to use your metal detector is not as easy as you might think. It’s illegal to use a detector in U.S. National Parks and historic battlefields. Many cities ban using them on public property or require you to apply for a permit beforehand. Make sure to check your local city and county laws to determine if and where you may be allowed to use a metal detector and if you’ll need a permit to do so.

And, of course, if you plan to use your detector on private property, you should obtain permission from the owner, or else you might dig up a lawsuit instead of treasure.

#6355. The brain’s protective barrier also blocks medicine. This engineer wants a way through

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

By Mandana Tadayon, Anna Mattson and Laura Sanders

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Rebecca Pinals hadn’t planned to study neuroscience. But as she watched her grandmother decline from dementia, the chemical engineer decided to apply her talents to the human brain.

At the time, “one of the big questions was, ‘how do we get access to it?’” says Pinals, of Stanford University. “I thought nanotechnology could be an interesting and useful toolkit to answer those types of questions.”

One key access point is the blood-brain barrier, a dynamic microenvironment of cells that helps keep pathogens and other contaminants out of the brain. It’s so good at its job that drugs for treating dementia have a hard time penetrating it. It’s important for researchers to understand this barrier, Pinals says, but it is so thin and fragile that they can’t observe it in real time without risking patient health.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Pinals and colleagues re-created the blood-brain barrier on a microchip. The team reprogrammed stem cells engineered from human skin, then coaxed the cells to form the barrier in a small 3-D chamber on the chip.

“As an engineer, this [system] is perfect,” Pinals says. “We love to take things apart and put them back together to learn how it’s made.”

Experts could use this scale model of the blood-brain barrier to figure out how to noninvasively access brains affected by neurodegenerative diseases. Pinals wants to use the device to investigate nanoparticles that could deliver drugs directly to patients’ brains.

#6354. The 6 Best Office Chairs for All-Day Comfort and Support

Need a better seat for your workspace? We have your back with these recommendations.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Your 40-hour work week is much easier on your joints and back if you’re sitting in the right office chair. For better or worse, the office chair might be the most important piece of furniture you own, given the sheer number of hours you spend sitting and working each day. An office chair that properly supports your back, neck, and shoulders can turn what could be a painful week into a comfortable one.

That said, a good office chair has to be a lot more than comfortable. Unlike loungers or couches, office chairs require upright support that promotes good posture for your back and neck. They also need to be flexible and mobile enough to move with you throughout a full work day, whether that’s leaning back during a quick break or rolling across the floor to grab something from the printer.

Choosing the right office chair means considering your body type and how long you sit at your computer or gaming desktop on an average day. Check out our list of the best office chairs for support and comfort, plus a few essentials to consider before you make your final decision.

We researched options across several major online retailers and compared their key specs, design, and adjustable features. We also looked at opinions from reviewers, real-life buyers, and users on online discussion forums such as Reddit. After narrowing our list to a few dozen qualified options, we pared it down further based on price and availability. Regardless of your budget or personal tastes and needs, you should be able to find a comfortable office chair.

This Branch office chair is modern, with an understated design and solid support features. What sets it apart from other options here is its six points of adjustability. That includes adjustable lumbar support to improve posture and prevent fatigue, and a back that tilts and locks for a more relaxed position.

The chair’s firm, cushioned base is slightly curved at the front and back to support a more natural seated leg position. The seat also adjusts forward and backward.

Considering the customizable settings for comfort and support, this office chair is a far better option than any others at this price point.

The Staples Dexley’s headrest slides up and down and tilts to line up with the back of your head. You can also move the lumbar support to match the curve of your lower back. The seat and back are both mesh, so you'll stay cooler on a long workday than you would in a padded chair.

The Dexley uses a synchro-tilt mechanism, which tips the seat and backrest together when you lean back. A tension knob sets how hard you have to push to recline, and the tilt lock holds the back in one of three positions. The seat height runs from 17.4 to 21 inches, and the armrests move up and down. The seat depth is fixed, though, so you can't slide it forward or back to fit your leg length. Staples says the chair can support up to 275 pounds over a 5- to 10-hour workday and covers it with a 5-year limited warranty.

The Hon Ignition 2.0 has a lumbar pad that moves up and down the backrest to meet the curve of your lower back. The pad is hard plastic, and a few Amazon reviewers said it pressed into their backs harder than they liked. The seat slides forward and back. That lets you set how much of your thigh the seat supports, whether your legs are long or short. The armrests change in height and width.

The back is mesh, which lets air through and keeps you cooler over a long workday. Hon rates the chair for 300 pounds. The Advanced Synchro-Tilt version on this listing lets you adjust how much force it takes to recline and lock the back in place.

Lock in and play all night long with this Secretlab gaming chair. With supreme comfort and all the standard adjustability features of office chairs, this model has a notably high back and wide sides for extra support. Its adjustable lumbar moves both up and down as well as in and out.

Because intense gaming requires focus, the chair must fit your body and posture closely. That’s why this chair, unlike any other on our list, comes in multiple sizes. The gaming chair also comes with a magnetic pillow you can attach anywhere on the back for extra comfort.

If you need extra head and neck support, this office chair is worth a look. The adjustable headrest cradles the back of your head and neck to help prevent strain and fatigue. The chair is covered in a breathable nylon mesh fabric that’s easy to wipe clean.

Other highlights include armrests that adjust in three different directions, plus it offers good lumbar support with adjustable height and width. The office chair also locks in a reclining position for sturdy yet relaxed support.

Most office chair armrests go up and down, and that's it. The Gesture's rotate a full 360 degrees, so they can swing in under your forearms when you're typing and stay there when you lean back to scroll on your phone. The back curves to follow the S-shape of your spine instead of pressing flat against it. Steelcase also built air pockets into the seat cushion, which it says ease pressure when you're sitting for hours.

You don't have to stand up or lean over to adjust the Gesture. All the controls sit on the right side of the seat. From there, you can slide the seat forward or back, set how hard you push to recline, or lock the back upright. The recline stops at three positions.

The Gesture holds up to 400 pounds, more than any of our other picks. The weak spot is the lumbar support. It's built into the back and doesn't adjust on this version. If lower-back support is your main concern, our lumbar pick gives you more control for much less.

A good office chair must be both ergonomic and supportive. Ergonomic design promotes good posture and keeps your body in an optimal position for focusing and working. Ergonomics and good posture go hand in hand with quality lumbar support. Office chairs with good lumbar support feature curved or cushioned backs that align closely with the natural curve of your lower spine, keeping you comfortable and upright for long stretches. Some office chairs have air pumps or adjustable curvatures to tailor the chair closely to your body.

Getting the right fit in an office chair depends on its adjustability. Most swivel and roll chairs have adjustable pneumatic bases that raise and lower the chair so your legs stay at a flat, comfortable level. Along with these basic features, some office chairs have an air pump for customizable lumbar support or attachable cushion straps or neck rests, and height-adjustable armrests that slide side to side.

Office chairs are typically made of polyester, leather, or cloth, plus foam. Most polyester or plastic chairs have lightweight, breathable mesh seats and backs that still offer solid lumbar support. Leather and cloth office chairs are typically cushioned for a bit more give. Foam gently molds to your body and may be more comfortable for your legs and back than mesh office chairs.

#6353. About three in four former NFL players who died from 2008 to 2023 had CTE

A new study estimates that about three in four former NFL players who died from 2008 through 2023 had CTE, even after accounting for brain donation bias.

Almost every former NFL player’s brain that researchers have examined has shown signs of chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), the degenerative disease tied to repeated hits to the head.

The study estimated that families were more likely to donate a player’s brain if he had clear cognitive symptoms.

Researchers at Boston University have now worked out how much that choice skews the picture.

The team’s estimate: about three in four NFL players who died between 2008 and 2023 had CTE. That includes the roughly five in six whose brains were not examined.

Three in four is lower than the figure from donated brains alone, where more than nine in ten had the disease. But the researchers said the skew in who donates can’t explain the high rate away.

Julia Gallini, a doctoral candidate in biostatistics at the Boston University School of Public Health, led the analysis with Yorghos Tripodis, a professor of biostatistics there.

Colleagues at the university’s CTE Center, Mass General Brigham and the Concussion & CTE Foundation joined them.

The figure applies to players after death only and says nothing about living former players or current ones.

Gallini said a precise number helps size the problem.

“An estimated 75% prevalence among NFL players who died over a 16-year period is concerning, and suggests we need to increase efforts to support families, diagnose CTE during life, and treat CTE-related symptoms,” she said.

CTE can only be confirmed after death, by examining the brain. So nearly everything known about it in football players comes from brains donated to a bank in Boston, and a 2017 study of 111 of them found CTE in 110.

Families don’t donate at random. A player who grew confused or forgetful in his last years is the one whose family thinks to call a brain bank.

So the donated brains carry more disease than the full population of former players would.

Epidemiologists call this selection bias. Earlier attempts to allow for it could only bracket the true figure somewhere between roughly 10% and 100%.

The team started with every former NFL player who died between January 2008 and December 2023, 2,362 men in all.

They were found through the National Death Index, the national register of death certificates. Of those, 396 had donated their brains and 1,966 had not.

The death certificates gave the researchers one fact they could compare across both groups: whether dementia was recorded as a cause of death. It was for 19.3% of donors and 11.2% of the others.

Because many people with failing memory die of something else, the team widened that category using survey estimates of milder cognitive trouble in former players.

Then they ran the comparison 1,000 times to capture the uncertainty.

The result was a ratio. A former player with clear cognitive symptoms was about five times as likely to have his brain donated as one without them.

Donors also died younger, at 67 on average against nearly 75. They had played longer too, seven years against under five.

Among the 387 donated brains with a clear verdict, 362 had CTE, or 93.5%.

After adjusting for differences in donation likelihood, the researchers estimated that 74.5% of all 2,362 players had CTE at death.

The team then tested how much that number depended on their assumptions. They restricted the sample to players who died at 55 or older, then 60 or older, and tried other definitions of who counted as symptomatic.

Across those versions, the estimate ranged from 70% to 86%.

The main figure sat toward the lower end of that range. The most conservative analysis put the figure at 63.7%.

Suppose symptomatic players had been ten times as likely to donate, rather than five. Even then, the authors calculated, more than 60% of the dead players would have had the disease.

CTE in the brain is not the same as symptoms in life.

Using the same correction, the team estimated that 27.2% of the players had a history of dementia before they died. In the donated group alone, the figure was 64.9%.

The authors said the true lifetime figure is probably higher than 27.2%. The donors it rests on died about eight years younger than the other players, with less time to develop dementia.

Many of the brains with CTE, they added, may have been at an early stage and symptom-free at death.

Matt Hasselbeck, an 18-year NFL veteran who serves as an ambassador for a research study called DIAGNOSE CTE, said the numbers read to him like a scouting report.

“I can’t take back the hits I took, but I can sign up for research and do whatever I can to help the scientists so they can find a cure in my lifetime,” he said.

The correction rests on a stand-in. Death certificates and survey estimates of memory trouble stood in for a direct look at the players whose brains were not examined. Dementia is also often left off a death certificate.

The authors also could not say whether CTE itself shortens life. That is one more reason the estimate stops at the dead and does not reach anyone still living.

Nothing here covers college or high school players, whose death records and symptom surveys don’t exist in the same form.

The authors said those estimates would be far harder to build, and that building them matters for sizing the problem.

Tripodis said the group recognizes the findings may worry living players and their families.

“Discoveries from the brain bank have already brought us significantly closer to a diagnosis during life, at which point our most important goal will be to develop effective treatments for CTE,” he said.

Until a living player can be tested for CTE, the dead are the only ones who can be counted.

The full study was published in the journal JAMA Network Open.

During a month-long excavation with the documentary series "Time Team," archaeologists unearthed another mysterious "sand body" at Sutton Hoo.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists have discovered a mysterious "sand body" at Sutton Hoo, an Anglo-Saxon cemetery in the U.K. that's famous for an enormous seventh-century ship burial of an early medieval king. The unusual grave does not have any bones but rather ghost-like shapes where a body was once buried.

Sand bodies were "burials where the bodies and bones had dissolved away in the acid soil, replaced by hard sand which held the form of the person, not unlike some of the bodies at Pompeii," Angus Wainwright, an archaeologist at the U.K.'s National Trust, said in a statement. These burials have been found at Sutton Hoo in the past, as well as at other Anglo-Saxon sites in the Suffolk area of the U.K.

The new sand burial, which was uncovered at a burial ground called Garden Field at the end of a 2025 dig, features in a four-part documentary created by the television series "Time Team" and archaeological experts with the National Trust and FAS Heritage. Whereas a 2024 excavation unearthed pieces of a bronze bucket used in a cremation ritual, the 2025 excavation was aimed at discovering evidence for the extent of the cemetery, when it was used and whether the people buried there were connected with the occupant of the famous ship burial.

"Until now, archaeologists have focused on the royal burial mounds," Wainwright said. In particular, experts have tried to work out who was buried in the "great ship burial" at Sutton Hoo. That person may have been King Rædwald, who ruled a kingdom in East Anglia and died around A.D. 627. The ship burial also contained an intricate and striking helmet. But the archaeologists are trying to learn more about the everyday East Anglians with the 2025 dig, which "moves the focus to these people and their ancestors and descendants," Wainwright said.

During the last week of the month-long excavation, the team unearthed the unusual sand body burial. Accompanying the deceased were grave goods, including beads, tweezers, a knife and a brooch, according to the statement. But directly underneath the sand body, the team found evidence that a second person may have been buried in the same grave.

"It was certainly a high point of this latest dig, to find another of these bodies in the Garden Field cemetery," Wainwright said. Experts think the sand bodies and cremations discovered in the burial ground may predate the famous ship burial.

In the first episode of a four-part Time Team series on Sutton Hoo, which launched on YouTube on Nov. 14, experts found new evidence that the people buried in the Garden Field cemetery were acquiring wealth and increasing their social status — so much so that they buried at least one person with a gold ingot.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The team also investigated the possible remains of a dock that was used to build and launch ships into the River Deben and found an unusual fragment of a cremation urn that surprised the archaeologists because it was decorated rather than plain.

"Well, it's at Sutton Hoo. Anything can happen," Justin Garner-Lahire, managing director at FAS Heritage, said in the video.

Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.

#6350. How one barley variety defends itself against crop pests and the virus they spread

In lab tests, fewer aphids settled on SY Kestrel barley, and those that did struggled to feed. The variety also slowed the buildup of barley yellow dwarf virus.

Aphids are known to feed on the sap of barley plants. During feeding they can also transmit barley yellow dwarf virus. Plants infected with this virus become yellow and stunted and produce less grain.

In response, breeders have introduced DNA from a wild relative of barley into commercial crops. Its protective effect was believed to operate mainly after the virus had entered the plant.

This wild DNA is carried by a commercial hybrid known as SY Kestrel. A new study found that the hybrid also makes it harder for aphids to settle and feed.

The aphids avoided its smell and fed poorly on its leaves and they also produced fewer offspring.

The research was carried out by Rumiana Ray’s group at the University of Nottingham. Scientists from Keele University and Syngenta were also involved in the project. SY Kestrel itself was developed by Syngenta.

Funding for the study came from Syngenta, and two of the authors are employed by the company.

All of the experiments were conducted on young plants in growth rooms and insect cages rather than in farm fields.

“What makes this discovery particularly exciting is that resistance is not simply about stopping a virus once it enters the plant. We have found that barley can defend itself at different stages of the aphid-plant interaction,” said Professor Ray.

In severe cases a winter barley crop can lose as much as 50% of its yield to the virus. According to the UK’s Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board, losses of this size are uncommon.

Chemical control is expected to become less effective over time. The authors linked this to growing insecticide resistance in aphids and to their lengthening migration periods.

The bird cherry-oat aphid is regarded as the main carrier of the virus. It picks up the virus from an infected plant and passes it on when it moves to a new one.

SY Kestrel contains a block of DNA from Hordeum bulbosum, which is a wild grass related to barley. Within this block lies a resistance region known as Ryd4Hb.

Earlier research had linked this region to the blocking of the virus once an aphid had delivered it.

For comparison the researchers used a second hybrid named Tektoo.

This hybrid was bred from the same mother line and from a very similar father line. Unlike SY Kestrel, it carries none of the wild DNA.

Aphids from a single laboratory colony were used throughout the experiments on both hybrids. Part of this colony had been allowed to acquire the virus beforehand while the remainder was kept virus free.

In the first experiment, 20 winged aphids were released into a cage that held one plant of each hybrid.

The positions in which the insects settled were then recorded at intervals over the following 24 hours.

Six cages were used in this test and the entire experiment was later repeated in full.

More than 75% fewer aphids settled on SY Kestrel than on Tektoo.

A large part of this difference could be attributed to the smell of the plants. In a separate test the air surrounding each plant was collected and offered to aphids with no plant present.

Under these conditions the insects were attracted to the odor of Tektoo but moved away from that of SY Kestrel.

The chemicals that made up each odor were then examined individually by the research team.

Heneicosane was one compound that was present in the air around Tektoo but absent from SY Kestrel. Aphids were attracted to heneicosane and those exposed to it subsequently produced a greater number of young.

In the air around SY Kestrel two compounds were detected that were not released by Tektoo. When they were tested separately both of these compounds were shown to repel the insects.

Infection with the virus was also found to alter the scent of Tektoo plants. Virus-free aphids preferred the odor of infected Tektoo plants while virus-carrying aphids preferred that of healthy plants.

This reversal has been interpreted in earlier studies as manipulation of the insect by the virus it carries. In SY Kestrel no comparable reversal could be detected by the researchers.

The odor of this hybrid repelled both groups of aphids regardless of whether the plant had been infested.

Despite the repellent odor a number of aphids did eventually settle on SY Kestrel.

Their feeding behavior was studied by attaching each insect to a fine gold wire. With this method the electrical signals from the mouthparts of each aphid could be recorded inside the leaf.

The recordings showed that aphids on both hybrids were able to reach the tubes that carry sugary sap. No meaningful difference was found between the two plants in how readily these tubes were reached.

After reaching the sap the aphids on SY Kestrel spent a longer time releasing saliva into the tubes. Sustained drinking of sap in bouts longer than 10 minutes was also markedly reduced on this hybrid.

This impaired feeding was associated with a reduction in the number of offspring produced.

On SY Kestrel the winged aphids carrying the virus produced about 40% fewer young than on Tektoo.

The survival of wingless aphids was also lower on SY Kestrel and their reproduction was reduced as well.

It is well established that plants rely on chemical defenses for protection against insects. In the leaves of SY Kestrel higher levels were found of three compounds that later proved harmful to aphids.

Each compound was tested by adding it to an artificial diet on which aphids fed for three days.

The compounds reduced the survival of aphids that were free of the virus. Aphids carrying the virus were less sensitive, and one of the compounds had no clear effect on them.

The team next examined plants that had been fed on by aphids carrying the virus. Fewer symptoms were seen on SY Kestrel than on Tektoo.

The amount of viral genetic material in the leaves of SY Kestrel was also much lower. By the tenth day the virus could no longer be detected. This measurement was based on three samples from each group.

The virus therefore faced three separate barriers in SY Kestrel.

Fewer aphids settled on the plant in the first place. The aphids that did settle fed poorly, and the virus they delivered failed to build up.

“Rather than relying on a single barrier, the crop can discourage aphids from settling, interfere with their feeding and restrict the virus they transmit,” Ray said.

The efficiency with which each leaf converted light into energy was measured as well.

This conversion represents the first step of photosynthesis and readings were taken daily from the second to the ninth day.

By the ninth day a decline in this efficiency had been recorded in Tektoo. The decline occurred in Tektoo whether or not the aphids feeding on it were carrying the virus.

A different pattern was observed in SY Kestrel when it was attacked by aphids carrying the virus.

In those plants the efficiency of light conversion remained close to the level recorded in plants without aphids. Feeding by aphids that were free of the virus did lower efficiency in SY Kestrel.

Changes in gene activity and leaf chemistry were recorded at the same time. Immune genes were involved in these changes along with the chloroplasts in which photosynthesis is carried out.

A group of fat-derived molecules that serve as stress signals in plants was affected as well.

According to the authors the continued function of the chloroplasts may help SY Kestrel to sustain its defense signals.

Several other plant viruses are already known to target the same chloroplast proteins. This has not yet been demonstrated for barley yellow dwarf virus.

SY Kestrel and Tektoo are not genetically identical outside the wild DNA. For this reason the authors acknowledged that some differences between the hybrids may originate elsewhere in their genomes.

The block of wild DNA carried by SY Kestrel is also considerably larger than the Ryd4Hb region itself. In a 2024 study, barley lines carrying a much smaller piece of this wild DNA were examined.

Complete resistance to the virus was observed in those plants. However, there was little evidence that this resistance depended on any change in aphid behavior.

Considered together, the two studies suggest that the smell and feeding defenses may depend on other genes.

Such genes may be located within the larger wild block or in other regions of the plant genome. They have not yet been identified.

The question is important for plant breeding. According to the authors, a smaller wild block may still provide strong resistance to the virus. Some of the defenses against aphids could be lost in the process.

“Understanding these complementary mechanisms offers new opportunities to develop crop varieties with broader and potentially more durable resistance,” Ray said.

Dr. James Melichar is the Hybrid Cereals Portfolio Lead Europe at Syngenta.

“This research demonstrates the value of bringing together commercial breeding expertise and fundamental plant science to understand how resistance operates in crops,” said Dr. Melichar.

“Identifying complementary mechanisms that affect aphid behaviour, feeding and virus infection provides valuable insights for developing barley varieties with broader and more effective protection.”

The diet tests also have a limitation. In these tests the levels of each compound were estimated from extracts of whole leaves.

Such estimates may not reflect the levels present in the sap that aphids actually consume.

Further research will be needed to identify the genes behind the defenses against aphids. The levels of the compounds in the sap itself will also need to be measured.

The full study was published in the journal New Phytologist.

#6349. Two stars in the Andromeda galaxy merged before astronomers’ eyes

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

A star called “Little Bao” danced with its giant partner “Big Bao”

An image captured by NASA’s Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer (WISE) telescope shows the Andromeda galaxy, which is the closest large galaxy to our Milky Way — and the home galaxy of Big and Little Bao.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

For seven years, a giant star in the Andromeda galaxy grew brighter. It swelled to more than twice its original size, even as its surface temperature barely changed. Then, in October 2025, it erupted. The slow brightening and sudden eruption tell a story of a smaller star orbiting inside of a massive star and what became of the pair, researchers report November 18 in Nature.

In work published last year, after poring through nearly 30 years of telescope data, astronomers had found that the giant began brightening in 2018 and proposed that a smaller star was circling ever closer around a giant companion and had even slipped inside its outermost layers. Astronomers call this elusive phase of a binary star’s life common-envelope evolution.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Now, the astronomers have analyzed the system’s dramatic next developments, culminating in the October 2025 eruption. (The stars are nicknamed Little Bao and Big Bao as a nod to that event’s official designation, AT 2025abao.)

First, astrophysicist Viraj Karambelkar of Columbia University and colleagues revisited those years of brightening given the imminent eruption. One cause of the brightening could have been gas flowing away from the stars, giving off light as it slowed down. But even if all the energy of that moving gas turned into light, it still wouldn’t be enough to explain the glow.

Instead, the researchers determined that the binary hypothesis they had originally proposed fit better: As Little Bao orbited inside Big Bao’s gas outer layers, the gas pushed back against the little star. That drag made Little Bao spiral inward and transfer energy to the surrounding gas. Some of that energy escaped as light, making Big Bao shine brighter.

Then, it was time to dig into what caused the eruption. If the outburst threw enough of the shared gas into space, the individual stars could have survived in an even tighter orbit. But the team estimates that only about a tenth of the giant’s outer gas escaped. The energy carried by that fast-moving gas also suggests that Little Bao reached Big Bao’s core. Together, those clues point to a merger.

Still, too much dust clouds the system to directly see what remains. And it won’t settle for years or even decades, although Karambelkar and his colleagues will be watching.

They’ll be looking for more examples of this type of merger, too. “Now we can go and try to look for similar systems,” Karambelkar says, “and hopefully aim to catch more of these systems even before they erupt.”

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

#6348. Young emperor penguins spend their first year at sea alone, so where do they go?

Satellite tags tracked young emperor penguins from three Antarctic colonies, revealing where they roam and when proposed marine protections could help.

Juvenile emperor penguins are left to fend for themselves at sea for roughly a year after they fledge.

The young birds receive no guidance from their parents during this time and many do not survive it.

Their routes were still found to be strikingly similar in a study of three colonies around Antarctica’s Weddell Sea.

The recurring pattern can help planners estimate when juvenile penguins would spend time inside proposed marine protected areas.

The study was led by Émile Brisson-Curadeau, a postdoctoral researcher at the Centre for Functional and Evolutionary Ecology (CEFE).

Daniel Zitterbart of the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution was a co-lead author. Céline Le Bohec of CEFE and the Centre Scientifique de Monaco shared that role.

“We were struck by the remarkable consistency of the penguins’ movements,” Brisson-Curadeau said.

Fishing vessel tracks were mapped as well, although the effect of fishing on the birds’ food was not measured.

Emperor penguins raise their chicks on sea ice that is attached to the coast of Antarctica.

The chicks develop waterproof feathers by late December and then leave for the open sea on their own.

Satellite tags were attached to 48 juveniles at the point when their new feathers had fully grown in.

A total of 28 birds came from Atka Bay at the eastern end of the Weddell Sea.

Around 8,000 pairs breed at that colony and its chicks were tagged over three summers between 2018 and 2023.

The remaining 20 juveniles were taken from Snow Hill Island and Jason Peninsula on the western side of the sea.

Each of these two colonies supports about 4,000 breeding pairs and their chicks were tagged during a single summer.

The movements of young emperor penguins from the western Weddell Sea had never been documented before this work.

Each tag was secured to the back feathers with tape and glue and weighed under 3% of body mass.

Most tags logged a position every four hours. Twelve of them also carried a pressure sensor for dive depth.

On average the juveniles travelled about 1,050 miles (1,688 km) from their colony at the farthest point of the trip.

The broad outline of this journey had already been described in earlier work carried out at Atka Bay.

No one had checked if it stayed the same across years, or across colonies on both sides of the sea.

In late summer, juveniles from Atka Bay, Snow Hill Island and Jason Peninsula all swam north.

By March, most had reached the waters just south of the Polar Front.

Here, cold Antarctic water meets warmer water from the north, and nutrient-rich upwelling feeds plankton and fish.

New sea ice starts forming in April. The penguins turned south to meet it and kept close to it all winter.

The ice reaches its greatest extent in August and September, and the birds moved north with its edge.

Once the ice began to melt, they headed back toward the continent.

By late December, most of the juveniles still being tracked had returned to waters near the coast, where they are thought to molt.

Multiple years of tracking were only available at Atka Bay, which made a direct comparison between years possible there.

Birds tagged in the same year were spread about as far apart as birds that were tagged in different years.

The authors suggest the juveniles may be following two stable features, namely the Polar Front and the sea ice edge.

From April onward the position of the penguins was closely linked to how far north the sea ice extended. Before April the birds were swimming in open water that lay far away from any sea ice.

A total of 52,710 dives were recorded by the pressure sensors over the course of the study.

The average dive reached a depth of about 220 feet (68 m) and lasted a little more than three minutes.

The deepest dive recorded in the study went down to roughly 1,155 feet (352 m).

Dives tended to be shallow at night and deeper during daylight hours. Deeper dives were also observed farther north and where more of the sea surface was ice covered.

The authors wrote that the birds may feed on lanternfish when they are near the Polar Front.

These small deep-water fish contain more energy than the krill and silverfish eaten by breeding adults closer to Antarctica.

Two marine protected areas are already in place in the region and two more have been put forward. The Weddell Sea proposal has been developed by Germany and the European Union since 2012.

If adopted it would become the largest marine protected area in the world and include waters near all three colonies.

Juveniles from the western colonies already spent part of their time in existing protected areas. This share was 20.6% for Snow Hill Island birds and 29.3% for Jason Peninsula birds.

Atka Bay birds spent only 2.3% of their time in such zones by comparison.

Atka Bay juveniles spent 31.6% of their tracked time in waters covered by the proposed protected areas.

Snow Hill Island and Jason Peninsula birds spent 21.0% and 14.7% of their time there.

Use of the proposed areas peaked in January, during the fledglings’ first weeks at sea.

Death rates among inexperienced juveniles are high in those first weeks at sea so the timing matters.

“Most marine protected areas in Antarctica are planned with penguin colonies in mind,” Zitterbart said.

“They protect the areas around the colonies, which is critical for adult penguins, but they fail to cover the sea areas where juveniles spend their vulnerable early years.”

Any new protected area in these waters needs the approval of every member of CCAMLR. This commission was set up in 1982 to conserve Antarctic marine life including krill.

Its members gathered in Hobart in October and left without agreeing on any new protected areas.

The main fishery in the region is aimed at Antarctic krill, which are small shrimp-like animals eaten by emperor penguins.

To estimate overlap the researchers relied on Global Fishing Watch, which is a public dataset of vessel activity.

It uses ship tracking signals to identify where fishing vessels are likely to be operating.

Fishing hours were totaled within about 62 miles (100 km) of each penguin location for the preceding year.

The waters used by juveniles from the two western colonies had more recorded fishing activity in the preceding year than the waters used by Atka Bay juveniles.

Much of this activity took place near the Antarctic Peninsula and in the waters around South Georgia.

Most of the overlap for these western birds occurred outside the boundaries of the planned protected areas.

Around Atka Bay the fishing effort stayed low for most months of the year.

January was the exception since the birds then used zones that had been fished heavily in 2022 and 2023.

Those zones are located within the proposed protected areas. Krill fishing there would be restricted to research and capped at one metric ton per vessel per year.

For comparison a typical fishing vessel in the region harvests about 40,000 metric tons over a year.

“Sustainable management of fishing activities, particularly their timing and intensity in key foraging areas, is essential to securing the food emperor penguins need and limiting the risk of bycatch,” Le Bohec said.

Around one third of the global breeding population of emperor penguins is found in the Weddell Sea region.

The IUCN moved the species to Endangered in April after projecting that its numbers will halve by the 2080s.

That projection rests largely on the expected loss of Antarctic sea ice.

The study measured overlap in space and time and not the direct effect of fishing on penguin foraging.

According to the authors direct studies of foraging success would give stronger evidence for the value of protection.

Tag losses also reduced the sample as the year went on and only 10 tags still reported in month 12.

Dive data were only available until September because none of the dive-recording tags transmitted beyond that month.

Sea ice extent was relatively stable between 2018 and 2024 including during an El Niño year.

Under continued warming the Polar Front is expected to contract toward Antarctica and winter sea ice could decline.

Juveniles might then travel shorter distances north but struggle to find suitable ice in winter.

A southward contraction would also raise overlap with the planned zones that are concentrated near the continent.

According to the authors it remains to be determined whether this would offset the effects of climate change.

Accelerometers could be used in future work to link penguin foraging success with fishing pressure.

Foraging and breeding success could also be compared before and after protected areas come into force.

The Weddell Sea proposal has not been adopted and most of the juveniles’ year is spent outside protected waters.

The full study was published in the journal Biological Conservation.

AI has upended the math community with a flood of results. We have to rethink how we assess which questions and answers matter — putting humans back at the center.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

An Anthropic mathematician using Claude claims to have proven the most famous problem in math — the Riemann hypothesis — in the latest, but potentially most consequential, example of artificial intelligence (AI) producing stunning math results.

AI has steamrolled its way into the math community. Anthropic's proof will certainly and rightly be scrutinized, but rather than picking apart every single result these models produce, we should respond by changing how we evaluate and reward expertise — placing less weight on the volume of results and more on the human judgment required to decide which questions and answers matter.

Without this shift, we risk drowning genuine insight in a flood of plausible but poorly understood mathematics.

This is a Live Science Pro article that we're putting out for free. If you liked this story, please consider subscribing.

Mathematical judgment is the ability to distinguish a result that is correct, but boring, from one that might fundamentally change how we think about the problem or even the whole area of mathematics surrounding the problem.

AI could generate hundreds of thousands of complex variations on a theorem, but these variations might add very little to mathematical knowledge, each one ultimately proving a dead end. A truly consequential result might settle a long-standing unsolved problem or connect to apparently unrelated areas. It is mathematical judgment that allows us to tell the difference between the two.

Earlier this year, an OpenAI system produced a counterexample to the long-standing planar unit distance problem, overturning a conjecture of Paul Erdős that had resisted mathematicians for decades. More recently, OpenAI announced an apparent solution to the Navier-Stokes problem, a celebrated question about whether equations describing fluid flow can develop singularities, or infinite values. It is one of the Clay Mathematics Institute's Millennium Prize Problems — a set of seven well-known and complex math problems, each with a $1 million prize attached.

Whether OpenAI's result ultimately stands up to scrutiny remains to be seen. But what is clear is that AI systems are now operating at a level that many mathematicians did not expect to witness for years, if not decades. OpenAI has since released hundreds of further mathematical results, leaving mathematicians scrambling to assess their correctness and significance.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

This does not mean that mathematicians are about to become obsolete. But it does mean we need to carefully reconsider what their precise purpose is.

Traditionally, expertise has been closely associated with production: Experts solve difficult problems, prove theorems, construct models and write papers. If AI can generate proofs, conjectures and probe research areas at unprecedented speed and scale, mathematical production is no longer necessarily the bottleneck. Instead, many pure mathematicians would argue that it is mathematical judgment that will become the scarcer resource.

Human judgment remains necessary because proofs generated by AI are not necessarily illuminating, comprehensible or even reliable. Some proofs may be so long or opaque that checking them requires substantial work by specialists and even more work to reinterpret them in a way that is meaningful to human mathematicians.

A proof can be valid without offering insight into why it is true or how its ideas might be employed elsewhere. The job of human mathematicians will be to become arbiters of the correctness of proofs, but also to scrutinize the reasoning and to extract the underlying ideas, determining whether the result says anything that meaningfully advances the field.

Mathematics, as a research community, needs to react rapidly to this change. Mathematicians and journals must prioritize significance over output. Mathematics involves deciding which results are important as well as generating them. A proof can be correct without being insightful. To give a simplified example, AI might "prove" that the square of a number divisible by two is divisible by four and then prove that the square of a number divisible by three is divisible by nine, and so on with ever larger integers. However, each new "proof" isn't an example of insightful mathematics, just a variation on the same elementary idea.

AI can create arguments faster than the community can verify, interpret or absorb them. Existing safeguards were not designed for that imbalance.

In contrast, a significant proof might settle a long-standing question, reveal an unexpected connection between disparate fields or develop a technique which is useful in the solution of many other problems.

Journals should therefore require authors to explain clearly what is genuinely new, why it matters — and what role AI played. Reviewers should judge whether a result deepens understanding, rather than merely verifying that the argument works. That does not mean rejecting work whose eventual importance is uncertain. The history of mathematics is full of ideas whose significance became apparent only decades later, so journals must continue to make room for foundational, exploratory and curiosity-driven research.

But there is a difference between a result with as-yet unknown implications and one that is unlikely ever to be insightful. Mathematical judgement cannot guarantee that nothing valuable is ever overlooked. It can, however, distinguish work that contains genuinely new ideas or possibilities from the automated production of uninteresting dead ends.

Universities and funders should also stop treating publication counts as a convenient proxy for quality. Careers are built around papers, citations, grants and prizes, but these measures were developed when producing sophisticated mathematics demanded substantial human time and effort. In the age of AI, work that might previously have taken years of careful thought could now be produced in weeks or even days.

Consequently, as the cost of generating mathematical results falls dramatically, those measures of quality become less useful. A decreased reliance on traditional metrics may be no bad thing, but institutions need credible alternatives: assessments of a researcher's most important contributions, evidence of intellectual leadership and explanations of how their work has changed understanding. This is urgent because mathematicians are already struggling to evaluate the sheer volume of material being produced.

Finally, mathematical training must continue to reward understanding. Written work alone will become a less reliable guide to individual capability when papers, reports and applications can be written mostly using AI. Seminars, discussions and collaborations can reveal whether someone understands an argument, can defend it and can connect it to other ideas. Demonstrating understanding has always been a more important quality in university students than simply presenting the answer; education and recruitment should now reflect that principle more explicitly.

Critics might argue that this is an overreaction. Mathematical claims still require proof, peer review already evaluates significance, and AI is simply another tool, like a calculator or computer algebra system. There is a degree of truth to each objection. Yet the explosion in the number of published papers changes the nature of the game. A calculator does not generate hundreds of research claims that specialists must spend precious time checking. AI can create arguments faster than the community can verify, interpret or absorb them. Existing safeguards were not designed for that imbalance.

Recent advances have understandably generated both excitement and anxiety. The right response is neither to reject AI nor to unguardedly celebrate every finding it produces. Journals, universities and funders should adapt their incentives now, before quantity overwhelms judgment completely.

In an environment increasingly capable of automatically generating research-level mathematics, the most valuable experts will be those who know which questions are worth asking, which results deserve trust and which ideas are worth our attention.

#6345. Permanent daylight saving time could send millions of kids to school in the dark

A new study estimates that permanent daylight saving time could add more than 2 billion trips to school before sunrise each year across the U.S.

Permanent daylight saving time sounds like more daylight. The hour doesn’t come from anywhere new, though.

It moves from the morning to the evening, and from November to March that would have millions of American schoolchildren leaving home before the sun is up.

Researchers at the University of Washington counted what that would mean, school by school, in 14 of the 19 states that have already approved the change.

The bill behind it, the Sunshine Protection Act, has passed the U.S. House but not the Senate, so the count is of a future that hasn’t happened yet.

Horacio de la Iglesia is a professor of biology at the university and the study’s senior author.

“It’s called the ‘Sunshine Protection Act’ because you get an extra hour of light at the end of the day. But you will take that hour from the morning. You could call it the Sunshine Destruction Act,” said Professor de la Iglesia.

Guadalupe Rodríguez Ferrante, a postdoctoral scholar in biology at the university, led a team that collected the actual start time of 16,093 public schools serving 8.6 million children.

Enrollment and locations came from the National Center for Education Statistics.

The team then worked out sunrise at each school on every school day. They ran it under three clocks: today’s system of switching twice a year, permanent standard time, and permanent daylight saving time.

A commute counted as dark if a child would have to leave home 20 minutes before the bell and sunrise hadn’t happened yet. The team added those mornings up across every child in every school.

Across the 14 states, permanent daylight saving time would add about 356 million dark school mornings a year compared with the current system.

Extended to every public school in the country, with a fixed 8 a.m. departure, the figure is 2.14 billion extra dark commutes a year.

In an interview with Earth.com, Professor de la Iglesia said the effect would reach nearly everyone.

“Parents should know that the number of mornings that their kids will go to school in the dark will increase dramatically under permanent DST. This will be true for virtually all children,” he said.

The hardest-hit places are not the northern ones. Georgia, which already has 75 million dark commutes a year under the current clock, would have 146 million.

Washington state would go from about 20 million to 55 million. Mississippi and Alabama, where schools start before 8 a.m. on average, would each go from about 2 million to more than 20 million.

What matters is where a school is inside its time zone. Sunrise comes later on the western edge of a zone, so Georgia, at the far west of Eastern Time, gets darker mornings than Maine at the far east of it.

Asked by Earth.com what surprised him most when the state numbers came in, Professor de la Iglesia named that pattern.

“That some of the hardest-hit States are not necessarily in a high northern latitude, like Georgia,” he said, and he put it down to Georgia’s position in its time zone.

Rodríguez Ferrante, who answered alongside him, said the average student in Georgia would leave for school before sunrise on about 86 school days a year under permanent daylight saving time.

In Washington state, much farther north, she said the figure would be about 52.

For a single child in Washington, the change is 28 to 39 more dark mornings a year, depending on the grade level.

The team then turned to a decade of fatal crash records, 2015 through 2024, from the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration’s FARS database.

They kept only school-year weekdays between 7 and 8:30 a.m., which left 10,305 fatal crashes, and 1,754 of them involved a pedestrian.

“Among fatal crashes during the morning school commute, the percentage involving a pedestrian aged 5 to 18 roughly doubled before sunrise,” Rodríguez Ferrante told Earth.com.

She said the analysis does not show that most such crashes happen in the dark, only that the crashes before sunrise more often involved a school-age pedestrian.

The figure for children rests on 141 crashes, so its range is wide.

The crash records show a pattern, not a cause. The authors wrote that the analysis is observational, that it counts only fatal crashes, and that the far larger number of non-fatal collisions is not in the record.

School districts have spent years pushing high school start times later because teenagers’ body clocks run late.

Permanent daylight saving time would move every start time an hour earlier relative to the sun without changing a single bell schedule, which the authors wrote would reverse those gains.

Morning light also does a job of its own. It helps set the body clock that regulates sleep, mood and appetite, and a child who leaves in the dark misses that cue.

De la Iglesia said he has heard the argument that schools could simply start later under permanent daylight saving time.

His answer was that everything else would then shift later too, work included, until everyone was back on solar time, which is what standard time already is.

“The U.S. tried year-round DST in 1974, and abandoned it within the year, partly because of dark winter mornings and concern for children traveling to school,” Rodríguez Ferrante said.

The count assumes every child leaves 20 minutes before class, and the national estimate assumes an 8 a.m. departure everywhere.

Both choices are on the late side, so the authors wrote that the true number is likely higher.

Children who arrive early for a school breakfast program, who are more often from lower-income households, would lose more mornings than the count shows.

The study estimated how often children would leave before sunrise. It did not measure how those darker commutes would affect their sleep or grades.

Rodríguez Ferrante said the bill passed the House in July and has stalled in the Senate, which adjourned for the midterm elections without acting on it.

The full study was published in the journal Current Biology.

#6343. NRCC Chairman Richard Hudson loses reelection in North Carolina

NRCC Chairman Richard Hudson, right, here at a hearing in June, lost his reelection bid in North Carolina's 9th District. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

North Carolina Rep. Richard Hudson, the chairman of the National Republican Congressional Committee, has lost his race for reelection, a stinging defeat for the man charged with preserving the House majority for the GOP.

Hudson fell to Democrat Richard Ojeda, a former West Virginia state senator who was leading  51 percent to 49 percent Thursday afternoon  when The Associated Press called the race in North Carolina’s 9th District.

Hudson had already conceded the race Wednesday, when it became clear that his path to victory was closing off.

“[The] voters of North Carolina’s 9th District made their choice and I respect it,” he said in a statement. “Since 2013 I’ve worked for North Carolina families. That includes the soldiers and families at Fort Bragg, who sacrifice more for this country than most people will ever know.”

Hudson is now the second party campaign chief to lose his seat during a midterm election this decade. In 2022, New York Rep. Sean Patrick Maloney lost reelection while serving as chair of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee.

Republicans across North Carolina experienced devastating losses on election night. As of Thursday afternoon, Democrats had also flipped the seats of Reps. Addison McDowell, Brad Knott and Tim Moore, as well as the open seat of retiring Rep. Chuck Edwards. The races for five other GOP-held seats remain uncalled, while Democratic Rep. Don Davis was reelected despite being targeted for defeat under a new GOP-drawn congressional map. Republicans also lost control of the North Carolina House and lost seats in the state Senate.

North Carolina’s 9th District, which includes the Eastern Piedmont region and the Fayetteville area, was far from the House battlefield for much of the midterm cycle. President Donald Trump carried the seat by 16 points in 2024, according to calculations by Inside Elections with Nathan L. Gonzales, and Hudson won a seventh term the same year by nearly 19 points. Hudson also held a financial advantage over Ojeda, raising $4.2 million to Ojeda’s $2.9 million through mid-October.

But in the waning weeks of the campaign, signs of Republican concern grew and Hudson’s campaign began spending on ads.

Ojeda was first elected to the West Virginia Senate in 2016. He ran for the U.S. House two years later as a Trump-voting Democrat but lost that race to Republican Carol Miller. He then briefly ran for the 2020 Democratic presidential nomination and also challenged GOP Sen. Shelley Moore Capito later that cycle but lost in the Democratic primary.

Ojeda moved to North Carolina in 2020, he told CityView, a local magazine, and he announced his challenge to Hudson last year.

Throughout the campaign, he attacked the incumbent over his support for Trump’s agenda, particularly the war in Iran. Ojeda is a retired Army major and the district is home to Fort Bragg, the nation’s largest Army base by population, where the Democrat was previously stationed for more than a decade.

“We did the impossible,’’ Ojeda told supporters Tuesday night. “We took on the chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee, a man with political connections, the billionaire donors, and the entire Washington establishment standing beside him.”

Hudson, 55, is finishing his seventh term in the House and his second term as NRCC chair. He had no primary opponent this year and had grown used to winning reelection by comfortable margins.

As a legislator, Hudson focused much of his policy agenda on health issues such as federal pandemic preparedness programs. He serves on the House Energy and Commerce Committee and chairs the panel's Communications and Technology Subcommittee.
