#6331. As Democrats look to next era, the veto and the filibuster await

Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer greets House Minority Whip Katherine Clark at the Center for American Progress Action Fund’s “Results to Roadmap” event on Thursday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

As Democrats continue their victory lap after their big wins on election night, outside groups and incoming freshmen are already turning up the pressure — and laying out competing visions of what the next two years should look like.

For Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer, it bears repeating that “the Democrats aren’t all exactly the same.”

“The most important lesson of this whole election, and one we all need to internalize if we’re going to truly build a durable majority, is populism and moderation are not mutually exclusive,” he said at a Center for American Progress Action Fund event on Thursday.

Voters are expecting results as Democrats claim a mandate to address costs and corruption. “Our majority will be measured against one test and one test only: Have we made your life better?” Schumer said.

He acknowledged, however, that their plans could run into a President Donald Trump-sized wall: the presidential veto.

“Will everything pass? Will Trump sign all of it into law? Knowing Trump’s and Republicans’  intransigence, of course not. But I will promise the American people: The Democratic Party will fight to make your life more affordable, your government more competent, your capital less corrupt, bill by bill, brick by brick, for as long as it takes for you to feel the difference,” Schumer said, hinting the road could be a long one.

But several progressive lawmakers and groups say the next Congress cannot be business as usual.

Indivisible, a progressive political organization that has described the Trump administration as a “fascistic clown show,” sent a memo to Senate Democratic offices Thursday morning urging them not to “squander” their momentum and to “fight at a level that matches the public’s demand for action.”

“Who leads the party in this era must be an open question, not a coronation. It’s time to define what the next era of the Democratic Party will be,” the memo reads.

The group has been encouraging voters to speak up and demand their senators hold “a contested leadership election, not a cleared field for Schumer.”

Meanwhile, Schumer has projected confidence he will keep his spot atop the caucus, especially after he helped pave the way for Tuesday’s blue wave. “I’ll be reelected as majority leader,” he said Wednesday. But the pressure campaign points to some tough math and harsh realities for the top Democrat — including some that mirror the woes of the outgoing Republican Majority Leader John Thune.

Among the demands outlined by Indivisible is one with a troubled recent history: “Breaking the filibuster on the first day of the new session.”

Democrats need to leverage “every procedural tool” if they “want the public to believe their campaign promises weren’t just more talk from politicians who are just like the old politicians they hated,” the memo reads.

The group isn’t alone in floating a new approach to the chamber’s 60-vote threshold for invoking cloture and ending debate. Some current and incoming lawmakers have signaled they would be open to going “nuclear” and abolishing the legislative filibuster, following in the footsteps of past majorities in both parties who have similarly changed how other Senate business is handled, like judicial nominees.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., argued in an op-ed in Time this week that Democrats could in some cases use existing tools, like a party-line process known as budget reconciliation, to pass their priorities. For non-budget items, like “bills to ban stock trading by federal officials or crack down on Trump’s corruption in plain sight,” Democrats should start by putting them up for a vote on the floor and letting “Republicans decide if they want to stay tied to such corruption.”

“And, if they do, then let’s clear away Senate filibuster rules and pass the laws anyway,” she wrote.

Sen.-elect James Talarico of Texas told NBC News on Monday ahead of his victory, “I believe the majority has the right to govern in this country, and the filibuster, which is not in the Constitution and is a Jim Crow relic, is leading to gridlock in our nation’s capital.”

Schumer ignored a question about nuking the filibuster at Wednesday’s event, saying instead, “The first thing we’ll do is reduce costs and work the legislative process.”

It would take 51 votes in the Senate for Democrats to go “nuclear” and establish a new precedent, a math problem that Thune knows all too well. The Republican from South Dakota faced loud criticism from conservatives online and hard-liners in his own party who said he wasn’t doing enough to try to pass a sprawling voter ID bill known as the SAVE America Act. But Thune repeatedly insisted he didn’t have the votes to change the chamber’s filibuster rules.

Many senators fear that blowing up the 60-vote threshold would fundamentally change the role of the Senate and its ability to tap the brakes on legislation that doesn’t have durable bipartisan support. Democrats went through a similar debate over the filibuster in 2022, during Schumer's first stint as majority leader. Even as others in their party pushed to pass sweeping voting rights legislation by any means necessary, Kyrsten Sinema and Joe Manchin, then moderate Democratic senators, held firm against filibuster changes.

And Schumer will have at least one Democrat on his hands who has already spoken up in defense of the filibuster, reversing his previous position. “I now recognize how important the filibuster is and the state our country would be in without it,” Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania wrote in a Washington Post op-ed earlier this summer, praising Sinema and Manchin as “courageous” holdouts who were wrongly “vilified” for holding the line.

None of that points to an easy ride for the incoming Democratic majority leader. And if fights over the filibuster weren’t enough, the caucus is also bracing for a different kind of intraparty angst, this time over impeachment.

The next likely House Judiciary Committee chairman, Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., told reporters on Thursday: “I have not had a single member of Congress or even a candidate say we’ve got to start out by impeaching Donald Trump.”

“For us, impeachment is not a fetish. It’s certainly not a taboo. We’ve impeached the guy twice,” he said, referring to Democrats’ efforts during the first Trump administration. “The problem has been over on the Senate side, and for us, it is a tool in the constitutional toolkit.”

Even if the House were to impeach Trump, a conviction would require a two-thirds supermajority vote in the Senate. And some Democrats are eager not to waste their hard-earned political capital on an impeachment quest that could alienate moderate voters and do nothing to bring down costs for everyday Americans.

Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, who boosted candidates in battleground races and recently released a roadmap for the new Congress, said at the CAP event on Thursday that lawmakers should “hold oversight hearings and expose the corruption of this administration. I’m not suggesting that that necessarily leads to impeachment. Maybe it does.”

Sounding more certain for Democrats in both chambers is their desire to impeach Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth over the war in Iran.

But that could be dealt with in the lame duck if Rep. Thomas Massie’s, R-Ky., resolution prevails next week. His proposal includes eight articles of impeachment, including allegations that Hegseth violated the 1973 War Powers Resolution in his prosecution of the Iran war and acted illegally in military campaigns in Venezuela, Yemen, the Caribbean Sea and the eastern Pacific Ocean.

Hegseth said in a video on Thursday of impeaching: “Didn’t work against President Trump. Won’t work with me. You can rest assured of that.”

Indivisible’s memo names impeaching Hegseth as a priority, as well as blocking a “business-as-usual” National Defense Authorization Act in the lame duck and refusing to fund the Department of Defense if “it doesn’t cut off money for the war.”

But it’s not clear that Democrats in Congress are ready to play that kind of hard ball. As they weigh their approach to the next era, they’re still half-stunned themselves by their larger than expected wins — and trying to put themselves in the best position ahead of the next elections in 2028.

GOP Rep. Christopher H. Smith of New Jersey told reporters on Thursday at the Capitol he hopes Democrats don’t hold up the NDAA “for the good of the country.”

“The NDAA is such an important bill for our national security, and it’s usually very bipartisan. I hope it is,” he said.

John Donnelly and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

#6330. U.S. demand for menopause hormone therapy has more than doubled recently

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Since 2023, monthly dispensing to women aged 40 to 74 grew from 2 million to almost 5 million

A woman applies an estrogen patch, one formulation of menopause hormone therapy. A study that finds a large, recent increase in hormone therapy pharmacy dispensing suggests more women are turning to the medication.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

More U.S. women are taking menopause hormone therapy, new prescription data suggest.

Monthly dispensing of hormone therapy for women aged 40 to 74 more than doubled since 2023, growing from 2 million to 4.9 million, researchers report November 19 in JAMA. The analysis of U.S. pharmacy dispensing data revealed that this increase began in 2024. The rise continued in 2025, before and after the Food and Drug Administration’s November removal of the black box warning from packaging, and into 2026.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Although the data in the new study are aggregate, the researchers used population data to estimate the dispensing rate for this age group, which jumped from 28 prescriptions per 1,000 women to 67 prescriptions per 1,000 over the period studied.

The new study wasn’t designed to determine what’s behind the increase. It’s possible that the evidence regarding hormone therapy’s safety and effectiveness for the treatment of menopause symptoms, such as hot flashes, is reaching more women. Medical groups such as the Menopause Society have recommended menopause hormone therapy for women with symptoms who are younger than 60 or within 10 years of the start of menopause, absent certain risk factors including prior breast cancer and stroke.

“Greater attention to women’s health, updated medical guidance supporting individualized menopause hormone therapy and social media may all be contributing to increased interest,” says Dana Sarnak, who studies sexual and reproductive health at Johns Hopkins School of Medicine. Anecdotally, her clinician colleagues report more patients seeking menopause care, she says.

Many women and physicians turned away from hormone therapy in the early 2000s after a large study called the Women’s Health Initiative raised safety concerns, which were later considered overblown. Research since then has provided a more nuanced understanding of the benefits and risks of menopause hormone therapy at different ages.

There are safer formulations, including patches and gels, of estrogen today then at the time of the Women’s Health Initiative, for which participants took a pill. The new study found that product use increased for transdermal and vaginal estrogen and for progesterone products — women who have their uterus need to take progesterone along with estrogen. The use of oral formulations remained stable. There has been a shortage of estrogen patches in the United States this year, which the U.S. Food and Drug Administration attributes to increasing demand.

#6328. The future of Caribbean coral reefs may be hidden in their past

Ancient coral fossils reveal more possible Caribbean reef habitat by 2100, but warming still threatens every species studied.

Predictions of coral survival in a warming Caribbean have generally been based on present-day reef records. Evidence from fossil reefs now suggests this basis has been too narrow.

In a new study, mid-Holocene coral fossils dated to 5,000 to 7,000 years ago were incorporated into habitat forecasts.

Four reef-building species were examined: elkhorn, staghorn, boulder brain and mustard hill corals.

More potential habitat for 2100 was identified once the fossil records had been included in the models.

The overall decline was not reversed by this additional habitat. Losses of 45% to 100% of suitable habitat were still projected for each species by 2100.

The extent of loss varied by species and by the level of future carbon emissions.

The research was led by Claire Williams at the University of Texas at Austin’s Jackson School of Geosciences.

Two variables were used to build the computer models: sea surface temperature and sea surface salinity.

Water suitability for each coral was estimated by these models. Actual reef growth at any given site was not predicted by them.

In habitat modeling, every recorded location of a species is paired with the water conditions measured there.

Maps of the future ocean are then searched for matching conditions.

Two limitations of models trained on present-day records alone were described by the authors.

Only water conditions found on Earth today can be learned by such models. Locations where a species is currently absent for other reasons are also missed.

Records from a different ocean are supplied by fossils. Caribbean corals have persisted through hundreds of thousands of years of changing conditions.

The fossil period selected here is regarded by researchers as an analog for present-day warming.

Coral occurrence records were obtained from public sources including the Paleobiology Database. Published reef surveys provided further fossil records.

Field observations collected in Jamaica between 2017 and 2024 were added by Williams’s team. At least 16 records per period were available for every species.

Fossil data are useful only if a species’ environmental tolerances have remained stable through time.

A closer match between past and present conditions than chance would produce was found for three species.

Elkhorn coral did not reach this statistical threshold. A large overlap between its past and present conditions was still seen.

Extra future habitat was picked up by the fossil-trained models for each of the four species.

As much as 44,200 square miles (114,559 square kilometers) of added habitat was projected for 2100. That is close to the size of Ohio.

No suitable habitat in 2100 was left for elkhorn or mustard hill coral by the modern-only models under high emissions.

Some habitat for both was kept once the fossil data were added. The authors flagged these estimates as highly uncertain.

The two sets of models were framed by the authors as the edges of a likely range.

Under high emissions, models based only on modern records found no suitable habitat for elkhorn or mustard hill coral in the study area by 2100.

Adding fossils revealed some potential habitat for both, though those estimates are highly uncertain.

Heat-stressed corals lose their color in a process called bleaching. Many of them die afterward.

The worst bleaching ever seen in the Northern Hemisphere came after record marine heatwaves in 2023.

Two emissions pathways were tested for each coral. Emissions level off near mid-century in one and keep climbing to 2100 in the other.

Habitat was lost by every species on both pathways. The losses grew under high emissions and from 2050 to 2100.

Boulder brain coral is a massive species that can live for a long time. Its losses were the steepest of all four.

No suitable habitat was left for it by 2100 under high emissions. Elkhorn coral was left with very little.

This clashes with the official threat status that boulder brain coral currently holds.

The species is ranked as vulnerable by the IUCN, the body that tracks extinction risk worldwide.

Elkhorn and staghorn corals sit one level higher as critically endangered species. Boulder brain coral may be more threatened than once believed, the authors wrote.

The largest share of habitat in 2100 was kept by mustard hill coral on both pathways. It is known as a weedy coral. It spreads easily but builds little reef structure.

Reefs made up mostly of this coral are expected to give less shelter to the sea life people rely on.

The models projected the heaviest habitat losses in the southern Caribbean.

All four species had lost their habitat near 10 degrees north by 2100 under high emissions.

A small patch near 15 degrees north was held only by staghorn coral. Most leftover habitat sat close to 20 degrees north.

The Florida Keys, Cuba and the north coast of Mexico’s Yucatán Peninsula still held habitat.

No real northward shift of the corals was detected. The southern habitat is simply lost and not moved.

Getting to the habitat that is left poses another problem for the corals.

Linked communities of mustard hill coral have been recorded more than 1,000 miles (1,700 kilometers) apart.

Elkhorn coral has been documented spreading only about 0.6 miles (1 kilometer).

Today, about 33% to 38% of modeled suitable habitat overlaps existing marine protected areas.

By 2100 under high emissions, the models projected that share would fall for mustard hill and elkhorn corals and rise for staghorn coral.

The models found no suitable habitat for boulder brain coral anywhere in the study area under that scenario.

New protected areas in the northern Caribbean were called for by the authors.

Closer ties between existing reserves were also urged. Mexico’s Sian Ka’an and the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary were named as examples.

Reef-dependent regions such as Jamaica and the Lesser Antilles are likely to lose all suitable habitat for the four corals studied by 2100.

Rowan Martindale is a co-author and associate professor at the Jackson School. According to her, those places cannot simply be abandoned.

Local communities rely on reefs for fish and for protection from hurricanes, she added.

What Jamaica has already lost was examined in a second study by Williams and colleagues.

Fossil and living reefs in northeast Jamaica were compared in the companion study.

These fossil reefs formed 125,000 to 130,000 years ago and are now exposed above sea level.

The surveys were therefore carried out on foot. Corals were photographed at intervals along measured transect lines.

Staghorn coral made up roughly half of the fossil coral on the seaward reefs at Navy Island and Dragon Point.

Elkhorn coral accounted for about 40% of the fossil community at Dragon Point and about 10% at Navy Island.

On nearby living reefs, the largely dead branching corals are now covered by algae. Mustard hill coral dominates the surviving coral cover.

Only sea surface temperature and salinity were included in the models. Conditions on the seafloor where corals grow may differ substantially.

Nutrient pollution, turbidity and ocean acidification were not considered in this analysis.

Coral disease and the decline of herbivorous reef animals were also excluded. Further habitat loss from these stresses was anticipated by the authors.

Future water conditions in the Florida Keys and along Cuba’s southern coast will be unlike any fossil or modern record.

Those areas are rated suitable by the models, yet corals may be unable to survive there. Future habitat is therefore likely overestimated.

Newer climate projections became available only after the analysis had been completed. A warmer and more saline Caribbean is indicated by them.

Smaller changes are projected for the Yucatán, which may allow suitable habitat to persist there longer.

“Conservation needs to be adaptive and to keep learning new information,” Williams said.

Fossils from older warm periods could also be incorporated, according to the authors. Unmatched future conditions would then be reduced.

Future research could also apply this method to reefs in the Indian and Pacific oceans.

The full study was published in the journal Conservation Biology.

#6327. Tiny reptile found in Wyoming sandstone is a prehistoric ‘dragon’

Neutron and X-ray scans revealed a tiny horned reptile inside Wyoming sandstone, offering a new clue to where its extinct relatives fit on the reptile family tree.

About 156 million years ago, the remains of a small horned reptile were buried in river sand in what is now Wyoming. Its head and body were found apart.

Its remains stayed hidden inside a slab of sandstone until scientists looked through the rock with neutrons.

Inside, they found a species nobody had seen before. Its tiny, almost intact braincase may help settle a long-running argument about where an odd group of extinct reptiles belongs on the tree of life.

The animal also has a name worthy of a heavy metal album cover.

The research was led by the Paul Scherrer Institute (PSI) in Switzerland and the University of Zurich, together with the Aathal Dinosaur Museum and the Swiss materials research institute Empa.

In January 2023, PSI materials scientist Pavel Trtik took his three sons to the Aathal Dinosaur Museum near Zurich. The boys loved the teeth and armor.

Their father was more interested in the rock. Trtik works at the PSI Center for Neutron and Muon Sciences. He uses neutrons to see inside solid materials.

On a whim, he left his business card at the front desk with a note: “If you ever have something you want investigated, just get in touch.”

Ten days later, the museum called. It had a fossil from the United States that nobody could identify.

A museum excavation team had found the fossil in August 2022 at the Meilyn Quarry in Wyoming.

That part of the American West has produced giants such as Diplodocus, Stegosaurus, and Allosaurus.

This find was much smaller. A row of tiny vertebrae showed in the sandstone, and the rest of the skeleton was still buried inside.

It could have been an early snake, a crocodile relative, or a baby dinosaur. Nobody could say which.

Neutrons turned out to be the right tool for the job.

“Neutrons are particularly sensitive to hydrogen,” Trtik explained.

“And hydrogen is also present in hydroxyapatite, a mineral component of bones. This allows us to distinguish the fossilized remains from the surrounding sandstone.”

The team also made X-ray scans at PSI, at Empa in Dübendorf and at the University of Zurich.

“The two techniques provide different kinds of information,” Trtik said. “Only by combining them can we get the clearest picture.”

They then sorted, combined, and interpreted tens of thousands of cross-sectional images. Slowly, the animal took shape.

They found pelvic bones, part of a hind leg and a tiny skull with an almost complete braincase. The skull turned out to be the real prize.

The reconstruction shows a reptile about 45 centimeters long with two horn-like spikes at the back of its head.

Its head and body were found apart, and fine sand buried both before the sand slowly turned to stone.

“It’s difficult to determine why the skull became detached from the torso,” explained Torsten Scheyer, the University of Zurich palaeontologist who co-led the study with Trtik.

“But we cannot rule out the possibility that a larger predator was involved.”

If a predator did take the head off, it was lucky for science that the skull wasn’t eaten or carried away by the current.

The braincase is less than two centimeters across, and it holds the most important evidence in the whole fossil.

The skull shows that the animal belonged to the choristoderes, a group of long-extinct reptiles. Later members of the group included long-snouted, crocodile-like river hunters, and some of them outlived the dinosaurs.

Paleontologists have argued for a long time about how choristoderes relate to other reptiles.

“The unusual shape of their skull bones has long made it difficult for palaeontologists to determine how they are related to other reptiles,” Scheyer said.

The new clue comes from the bones of the inner ear.

“They bear a striking resemblance to those of the so-called crown group of reptiles, which includes all living reptiles,” the palaeontologist explains.

“This could suggest that choristoderes are more closely related to living reptiles than previous fossil evidence indicated.”

The little reptile is also a new species. It is the most complete early member of the choristodere group found so far, and the oldest one known from North America.

Scheyer is a big fan of The Lord of the Rings and of hard rock, and both shaped the animal’s name.

“When I looked at the three-dimensional images of the little reptile, with its head possibly torn off, I knew straight away: such a spectacular creature deserves an equally spectacular name.”

He called it Meilynodraco amonamarthi. The first part means roughly “Dragon of Meilyn,” after the quarry and the horns on the back of the head.

The second part honors his favorite band, the Swedish melodic death metal group Amon Amarth.

The band took its name from Tolkien, since Amon Amarth is the Elvish name for Mount Doom, the volcano where the One Ring was made and finally destroyed.

The fossil will go on display in early 2027 in “Rock Fossils on Tour,” a traveling exhibition at the Aathal Dinosaur Museum.

“The little dragon will be in excellent company here, with other spectacular fossils named after famous metal musicians and rock bands,” said the museum director Yolanda Schicker-Siber.

PSI hopes to scan much bigger fossils in future. A proposed test facility called UFO, short for “UltraFast neutron irradiation for large Objects,” would fit objects up to a meter long.

It is being considered as part of a possible upgrade to PSI’s neutron source.

The study is published in the journal Royal Society Open Science.

The brains of people with PTSD bear molecular changes that differ from those in people with other conditions, like depression, a new study finds.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A study of hundreds of brains has revealed molecular differences in people with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) that are not found in individuals without the condition.

These molecular marks also differ from those seen in the brains of people with other conditions, like depression, the research found.

Our environment and experiences influence how our genes work, affecting which genes can be turned on. Rather than changing genes' underlying code, the environment can trigger what are known as epigenetic changes, which include certain chemicals that attach to DNA molecules and change their structure.

One such epigenetic change, called methylation, can work like a "dimmer switch" for genes, or even completely block certain genes from turning on.

"These epigenetic features of the brain are important for shaping the way the brain functions," study co-author Frances Champagne, a psychologist at the University of Texas at Austin, told Live Science. "This can give us some insight into why individuals with PTSD develop PTSD, or how [their brains] are different from a healthy brain."

In the new study, published Friday (Nov. 20) in the journal Cell Reports, scientists took a close look at DNA methylation in 302 brains that had been donated after death. These included 101 brains from individuals diagnosed with PTSD, 101 from people with major depressive disorder and 100 from people without any diagnosed psychiatric disorders. The researchers also had access to these individuals' medical records.

The team zoomed in on three brain regions: the prefrontal cortex, the amygdala and the hippocampus. The prefrontal cortex handles cognitive functions like planning and decision-making, the amygdala is a major hub for emotional processing, and the hippocampus is key for memory and learning.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"The goal of our study was to look at the epigenetics of the PTSD brain and ask how [it] is different from that of an individual who does not have PTSD," Champagne said, "or who comparatively has another diagnosis, like major depressive disorder."

Compared to the brains of people without any disorders, the brains of people with PTSD had different patterns of methylation in the prefrontal cortex, in particular. By contrast, in major depressive disorder, the amygdala stood out as a brain region with distinct methylation.

Additionally, in depression, the observed differences in methylation tended to affect the same set of genes across different regions of the brain. This was not the case in PTSD, which showed more inconsistencies in terms of which specific genes were involved. The methylation patterns in PTSD also appeared to vary depending on other factors, such as patients' sex, ethnicity and age at which they experienced trauma.

The study's results serve as a valuable resource, said Seyma Katrinli, an investigator in the Grady Trauma Project, a large PTSD study, at the Emory University School of Medicine.

Although the findings can't be used to help diagnose PTSD yet, down the line, this area of research could help scientists correlate changes that are measurable in people's blood to changes in the brain, said Katrinli, who was not involved in the new work. Then, blood tests could help guide the diagnosis and treatment of PTSD, she suggested.

That said, the study had limitations. Because the scientists analyzed postmortem brains, they relied on the medical reports rather than assessing the study subjects directly. Additionally, both PTSD and major depressive disorder are associated with substance use, which also causes DNA methylation; this potential confounding factor was not accounted for in the study. .

Finally, at this point, there is no way to tell what triggered the observed differences in DNA methylation. The scientists can't say if the variations are a consequence of PTSD, a risk factor for PTSD, or a downstream effect of other things that co-occur with PTSD.

The research sets the stage to "help us ask better questions," Champagne said. Her team is now looking to investigate factors — such as sex, the timing of traumatic experiences, or history of substance use — that may be driving the variation within PTSD.

"It's a very exciting foray into epigenetic profiling in the brain," she said.

DNA methylation profiling of human brain in posttraumatic stress and major depressive disorders indicate specific molecular features. #6324. Meeks vows Iran votes as he seeks Foreign Affairs gavel

Rep. Gregory W. Meeks, D-N.Y., and staffers cheer as House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., takes the stage during a election night watch party in Washington on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Rep. Gregory W. Meeks, D-N.Y., the presumed next chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, plans to bring resolutions to the floor to “immediately” end the war with Iran when Democrats take control of the House in January, he wrote in a letter Thursday seeking his colleagues’ support to become chairman.

The letter, which officially announced his bid for the chairmanship, lays out his oversight agenda for the committee, which will also see considerable turnover on the GOP side of the dais.

Meeks and other Democrats have repeatedly forced votes this year on war powers resolutions seeking to end the Iran war, with a Meeks-sponsored one clearing both chambers of Congress.

But those resolutions have been nonbinding concurrent resolutions, since the 1973 War Powers Resolution only lays out a fast-track procedure the minority party can wield for concurrent resolutions in the House.

With a House majority, though, Democrats could bring binding joint resolutions to the floor.

Beyond war powers votes, Meeks also promised public hearings on the war. He also vowed hearings on a range of topics including the administration’s Venezuela policy and “repeated defiance of Congress's constitutional authority over war powers and trade.”

“As chairman in the 120th Congress, oversight of this administration’s lawlessness and corruption will be at the top of the agenda,” Meeks wrote. “I will continue to advance a principled foreign policy grounded in our values, including support for Ukraine against Russian aggression.”

In addition to Iran measures, Meeks also promised legislation focused on “clawing back Congress’s proper role in the making of American foreign policy” and a State Department reauthorization bill that puts guardrails on the administration and protects career diplomats.

Meanwhile, the GOP side of the committee is poised to lose at least a dozen lawmakers — or about half of its members — next year between retirements and election losses.

The departures include longtime members such as former Chairman Michael McCaul, R-Texas, who opted not to seek reelection, and Rep. Scott Perry, R-Pa., the Freedom Caucus chair who lost his reelection race.

Several other Republican committee members remained locked in races that were still too close to call as of Thursday afternoon, according to The Associated Press, potentially gutting the GOP committee bench further. They include GOP Rep. Young Kim of California, the East Asia and Pacific Subcommittee chair who was trailing her in race against fellow California Republican Rep. Ken Calvert.

Rep. Christopher H. Smith, R-N.J., who chairs the Africa Subcommittee, lamented the turnover Thursday but predicted a lot of interest among remaining House Republicans to fill the void.

“There will be many who will want to be on it,” Smith told reporters. “We lost some really great people. Yesterday I can't tell you how sad I was about friends who are now not coming back.”

#6323. Hubble caught a spiral galaxy from an angle that hides its arms

Hubble’s edge-on view of spiral galaxy NGC 1827 reveals dark dust lanes, a bright central bulge and blue patches where stars may be forming.

Today’s Image of the Day from Hubble shows a ribbon of rust-colored dust cutting through a bright band of starlight.

The ribbon breaks into dark patches toward the edges, and it takes a moment to recognize what you’re looking at: a spiral galaxy seen from the side.

The galaxy is NGC 1827. From this angle, the arms that would sweep around its center in a face-on view overlap along our line of sight.

What stands out instead is the structure of the disk itself, from its glowing central bulge to the uneven ribbon of dust that runs through it.

NGC 1827 lies about 37 million light-years away in the constellation Columba, also known as the Dove.

Hubble captured this view with its Advanced Camera for Surveys, and NASA released the image on October 16.

A spiral galaxy’s disk is wide and relatively thin. Its arms curve through that disk, carrying stars, gas and dust.

When we see the disk nearly edge-on, much of that material appears in a narrow strip.

The central bulge, which extends above and below the disk, gives the galaxy its thicker middle.

That geometry also makes the dust especially easy to see. Along parts of the disk, we look through enough dust to dim the combined light of the stars behind it.

The resulting dark lane runs in front of the bright bulge, where the difference between the obscured and unobscured regions is easiest to make out.

Follow the dust lane away from the center and you’ll see bright blue patches scattered across the disk. NASA identifies them as places where new stars are likely forming.

Hot, massive young stars give off intense blue light. They burn through their fuel quickly by stellar standards, so a concentration of them can point to relatively recent star formation.

In NGC 1827, those blue patches sit among dark clouds, where gas and dust provide the raw material for future generations of stars.

The side view makes it difficult to tell which arm a particular patch belongs to.

A knot of blue light that appears close to the center in the image could sit farther out in the disk, somewhere along the same line of sight.

Hubble shows where each feature appears in the image, but its true distance from the galaxy’s center is harder to pin down.

Just left of the galaxy’s bright middle, a star stands out with four sharp spikes.

It looks close enough to belong to NGC 1827, but it lies between Earth and the galaxy. Its apparent position is a chance alignment.

Those four spikes offer a clue to another kind of structure, this time inside the telescope. They appear when light from a bright point source bends around the supports that hold Hubble’s secondary mirror in place.

The pattern is especially obvious on this star because so much of its light comes from one tiny point in the image.

Other objects sit much farther away. Look into the dark sky beyond the disk and you’ll find small, faint smudges, some of them distant galaxies.

A single frame brings together a foreground star, a nearby spiral and galaxies deeper in the background.

The portrait came from a Hubble program targeting 260 satellite galaxies around 22 hosts similar to the Milky Way.

These smaller galaxies give astronomers a way to test how well models of the universe describe what happens on the scale of individual galaxies and their neighbors.

Computer models can reproduce many of the broad patterns astronomers see across the universe.

The details get harder to match on smaller scales, where the growth of galaxies depends in part on how gas gathers and how stars affect the material around them.

Looking at many satellite systems gives researchers a broader sample for those comparisons.

Hubble’s sharp view is useful because a galaxy’s overall brightness tells only part of its story.

In this image, the narrow dust lane, bright central bulge and scattered blue patches each give a different view of how its material is arranged.

From another vantage point, the spiral arms might be the first thing we’d notice.

From Earth, the most striking feature is the dark streak down the middle, visible because the galaxy’s own stars light it from behind.

#6322. A brain region known for listening helps us speak

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Recordings reveal how Wernicke’s area helps turn thoughts into words

A small bit of brain has big roles in understanding and producing speech, a new study finds.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

WASHINGTON — A part of the brain famous for listening is important for talking, too.

Data collected from people as they listen and try to talk show that this brain region, a small spot inside a larger area called Wernicke’s area, has a more expansive job than researchers thought when it comes to communicating. The results may help efforts to restore people’s voices. The results presented November 15 at the annual meeting of the Society for Neuroscience and published November 19 in Science.The study provides convincing evidence that this brain spot is critical for speech production, says neurologist and language researcher Jeffrey Binder of the Medical College of Wisconsin in Milwaukee. “My hope is that this study will help scientists and clinicians accept a more accurate interpretation of this focal area” as an early stop on the pathway to saying a word.

A small part of the brain, just above the left ear, was first described in 1874 by a neurologist Carl Wernicke as necessary for making sense of speech. People with damage there had trouble comprehending words. But some people also had trouble producing them. “Sounds were swapped, words were replaced with near misses,” Edward Chang of the University of California, San Francisco, said in a news briefing. “The basic question has been, ‘Why would damage to a hearing area of the brain break the ability to speak?’ That question has been open for 150 years.”The new research offers an answer: A small bit of Wernicke’s area (to be extremely specific, the left posterior superior temporal gyrus or lpSTG ) becomes active just before a word is spoken. “Every word that you have said today began in that small part above your left ear about a quarter of a second before you said it,” Chang said.

The finding adds to growing evidence that brain areas are more complex than people have appreciated, says neuroscientist Leigh Hochberg at Brown University in Providence, R.I. “I believe that one of the things we are going to learn over the next five, 10 years of this research, is that each part of the brain that, we were taught as a med student or a grad student, does this, probably does that and a whole lot more.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Scientists measured brain activity in 28 people before they had surgery for epilepsy or tumors. They were able to see that this brain region kicked on as a person listened to words, and also just before they attempted to speak. Cells there had preferences for certain sorts of words, long ones, for instance. “It’s more active when you’re about to say the word caterpillar than when you’re about to say the word cat,” said Matthew Leonard, a cognitive neuroscientist at UCSF.

Electrical stimulation to this small bit of brain also interfered with people’s ability to talk. “What we found was that stimulation, really only in this lpSTG area, disrupted this speech production when it was delivered just prior to speaking,” said UCSF bioengineer Alexander Silva.

Some efforts to make implanted devices that can help restore speech to people who no longer talk focus on the motor cortex, a part of the brain that controls the movements required for speech. This bit of Wernicke’s area offers an additional spot to consider, Silva said. “What if you could target a single brain region and gain access to the full spectrum of speech, from listening all the way up to speech production?”

Experimental brain implants in two volunteers with paralysis were able to detect both what they heard and what they were trying to say, the researchers report in the study.

The discovery may help scientists better understand situations that involve both hearing and speaking, such as speech or comprehension differences in people with autism, or how children first begin learning to talk, Chang said.

#6321. The 6 Best Electric Snow Shovels for Quickly Clearing Sidewalks and Driveways

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

These models deliver fast cleanup with minimal effort when there isn't enough accumulation to take out the snowblower. Here are our recommendations.

Winter will be here before you know it. Easily one of the most laborious and hated chores of that season is shoveling the snow. Not only that, it can be dangerous. Beyond the strain it puts on your back, the American Heart Association says it can increase the risk of a cardiac event for those with heart issues, and the cold weather can hide symptoms that otherwise would give you pause. That’s why the best electric snow shovels not only make the task easier, but safer, too, for those at risk.

Of course, you should not mistake these for full-blown snowblowers. Because of their compact size and throwing range, electric snow shovels are best used for small homes with shorter walkways and fewer steps. Like their larger counterparts, they use augers to scoop up snow (no more than 6 to 8 inches, ideally) and launch it up to 25 feet through the air so you don’t have to bend or lift as you dig out after a storm.

They also work well as supplemental tools for clearing out outdoor stairs, walkways, patios, decks, and anywhere else a snowblower may not be able to reach. If that sounds like it could help you out of a blizzard-induced jam this winter, we can steer you toward the best electric snow shovels that can make the chore as painless as possible.

Toro Power Shovel 60-Volt 12-Inch Electric Snow Shovel

As a top name in yard tools, we are interested to see what Toro’s take on simple snow removal is.

Ego Power+ EGO POWER+ 12-Inch Electric Snow Shovel

Ego has several models of electric now shovels. This one has adjustable fins to let you guide the direction of the snow you remove.

We leaned on our personal experience with snow removal machines and conducted extensive research to inform our selections. Specifically, we looked at each machine’s clearing area, weight, battery life, and throwing distance. Because snow removal needs vary from property to property, we included larger models that can clear up to 6 inches of snow from two- to four-car driveways, along with lighter electric snow shovels that are easy to lift and maneuver in smaller areas, such as walkways and patios.

Though we still include one corded model as our best budget pick, we primarily focus on cordless models because for most people these days, the convenience of battery power beats having to drag a cord around on a cold day.

Most electric snow shovels max out with a fairly narrow clearing width and low clearing depth, potentially forcing you to do multiple passes to clear a proper path. This Earthwise model is an exception.

With a broad clearing width of 16 inches and a depth of 8 inches, it’s capable of clearing paths through deeper snow. And since it launches snow up to 32 feet away, you can use this machine to clear small driveways along with your walkways, deck, and patio.

On the other hand, this electric snow shovel is quite heavy. It has wheels, though, which make it easier to push and maneuver. It’s a tradeoff, but one that pays off if you live in an area that routinely gets 6 to 8 inches of snow in a night.

You may notice that our best overall is a bit cheaper than our best value pick. This is because we felt the wide clearing width and the fact that it has wheels to support your efforts made this a solid choice for many people.

Though higher in price than some of the other models on our list, there’s a lot that you get for the price, namely power and run time. With a larger battery than most, this electric shovel from Greenworks runs longer on a single battery than any other cordless electric snow shovel out there.

It packs a good amount of power with a large 80-volt 4.0-amp-hour battery powering a brushless motor; you’ll get about 45 minutes of run time on a single charge. This snow shovel clears a 12-inch path through up to 6 inches of snow, then blows it 25 feet away, making it ideal for uncovering a large area after a light snowfall.

Just remember that with great power and runtime comes great weight. With the battery loaded, this machine weighs more than 19 pounds, so moving it around for 45 minutes can turn into a real workout.

If you want the most clearing power possible from an electric snow shovel, Earthwise is your brand. This corded model can carve a 16-inch-wide path through snow up to 8 inches high, which is significantly more than what you can expect from other brands. It’s also significantly more powerful, moving up to 430 pounds of snow per minute.

For reference, most of our other picks move around 300 pounds per minute. As a result, it can handle deeper, slushier snow than most electric snow shovels. It also has a longer throwing distance than most corded or cordless electric snow shovels out there.

At 16 pounds, it’s pretty heavy, but like other heavy models, it has a pair of wheels so you can push it most of the time. In short, it offers the best snow removal capability of any machine this side of a snowblower.

Ryobi makes several types of cordless electric snow shovels, but this model is a head attachment for its Expand-It 40-Volt String Trimmer that you can swap in when the snow starts falling. The advantage here is that you aren’t limited to just one tool; you can swap in a variety of attachments to run on the same primary unit and battery. This makes a lot of sense if it only snows a couple of times where you live, and you only need a snow thrower infrequently.

During our testing, we were impressed with this tool’s performance. In mere minutes, we were able to clear a wide path through 8 inches of snow (more than the max height of 6 inches this model is rated for) on a patio outside our office. It was not fresh snow, either; it was densely packed after sitting for several days. There were times when the shovel head froze up while trying to push through too much at once, but this was quickly rectified by pulling back and pushing through again. The snow flies quite far, too, for such a small toolhead, at least 10 to 15 feet by our estimation.

Being able to fling snow that far is a good thing because this thrower can only send the snow straight forward (some models have adjustable fins that allow you to send it to either side). You need to be strategic about the direction you push to avoid creating more work for yourself if you have a long path to clear.

We must admit, too, that while this electric snow shovel makes the job easier than a manual shovel, it does take a bit of strength to operate, especially since it doesn’t have wheels to help you stay balanced and moving. You can move it along the ground, but you may need to lift it slightly if the snow is packed or icy at the lower levels, and it doesn’t come with a shoulder strap to help you do that. If you aim to greatly reduce the physical strain of snow removal, models from our list that feature wheels and directional fins may be a better option.

Overall, if you already have the Ryobi 40-volt-compatible string trimmer, adding this attachment to your arsenal would be a good move if you only need to clear snow from a small driveway, walkway, deck, or patio. The 40-volt, 4-amp-hour battery will give you up to an hour of power, which is more than enough for a small job like that, and buying into this multitool system will keep it from being a tool that just sits in the toolshed or basement for most of the time.

The lightweight design of this cordless electric snow shovel makes it a great option if other electric snow shovels are too heavy for you to manage. Whereas most electric snow shovels weigh around 18 pounds, this one weighs just 13.5 pounds.

Along with being lighter, the Snow Joe electric snow shovel also has a dual-handle design that allows you to operate it while standing up straight, taking pressure off your back. Despite its lighter weight, it can still clear a foot-wide path of snow up to 6 inches deep. The Snow Joe does have a shorter runtime than most, which limits it to lighter-duty snow removal, such as clearing walks, decks, and patios.

With its two 20-volt rechargeable batteries, the Worx electric snow shovel is both versatile and powerful. It can clear a path a foot wide and up to 6 inches deep and throw snow up to 25 feet, so it's suitable for clearing tighter spaces.

The two-battery design gives you the option to mix and match larger-capacity 20-volt Worx batteries to increase this shovel’s run time for larger jobs, such as clearing small driveways. It also comes with a dual charger, so you can charge both batteries simultaneously for a shorter turnaround time.

Another plus is that this model's batteries are compatible with other 20-volt Worx yard machines, making it a great option if you’ve already bought into the Worx product line.

We’d be remiss if we didn’t point out that this whole category of yard machines has some limitations. Most electric snow shovels can only handle snow depths up to 6 inches—8 inches if you’re lucky—and lack the power to handle heavier slushy snow. They are ideally suited to powdery snow on walkways, patios, decks, and maybe a small driveway. If you see heavy snowfalls regularly or have a large number of driveways and parking spaces to clear, get a snowblower before you buy an electric snow shovel. For big jobs, go with a gas snowblower. An electric snowblower works for small to moderate-sized driveways.

When push comes to shove, we recommend looking for a cordless electric snow shovel rather than a corded one. Having the freedom to move without worrying about a cord makes the whole shoveling or snowblowing process much easier. That said, if you’re on a tight budget or only need to clear a short walk or a small patio or deck that’s near an outdoor outlet, you can get by with a corded model.

Much like a snowblower, electric snow shovels are rated by how much snow they can move. The wider the shovel, the fewer passes it takes to clear an area. Most electric snow shovels move a 10- to 16-inch-wide path of snow. A small, narrow shovel is lighter and more nimble, making it useful for creating pathways. Wider, larger models are better equipped for clearing a patio or driveway, but are also heavier and more difficult to maneuver in tighter spaces.

Electric snow shovels can handle snowbanks around 4 to 8 inches high, depending on their clearing depth. Technically, you can remove deeper snowfall with these machines, but you’ll have to make more passes to do so.

For an electric snow shovel to be useful, it should be able to propel the snow far enough that it’s off the deck, walkway, or driveway that you’re clearing. Most electric snow shovels launch their snow between 20 and 30 feet, which is on par with entry-level, corded electric snowblowers, but shorter than cordless and gas snowblowers that can throw snow a distance of 40 feet or more. With that in mind, consider the route you plan to take while clearing, and make sure you’re moving the snow somewhere out of the way so it can sit until spring arrives.

Electric snow shovels process and throw snow like a snowblower, so you won’t need to bend over and scoop up snow as you would with a shovel. However, you should still look for the lightest possible option. While you won’t have to lift and throw snow as you would with a conventional snow shovel, you have to hold it upright and apply some force to push it through the snow. At the very least, you should look for a shovel that you can lift easily whenever you need to clear steps or multiple levels of patio.

Electric snow shovels typically weigh between 10 and 20 pounds. As you might expect, more powerful shovels that can move more snow and feature large batteries tend to be heavier than smaller, narrower models. Some large electric snow shovels have a set of wheels mounted to the rear of the base for standing upright on their own, so you can maneuver the machine with minimal lifting.

Similar to standard snow shovels, electric models come in both straight and curved handle varieties. A curved handle allows for standing more upright while operating the machine, putting less strain on your lower back and decreasing the risk of injury. A straight handle gives you more leverage for lifting loads of snow, but since an electric snow shovel has an auger that lifts and blows the snow for you, it’s not an advantage for electric models.

Electric snow shovels operate similarly to single-stage snow blowers. The shovel end of the machine has an auger that’s powered by an electric motor. As you push the shovel through the snow, the rotating auger collects snow, mashes it up, and then propels it through a shoot that throws the snow off to the side

The average electric snow shovel can churn through about 300 pounds of snow per minute. That means a snow shovel with a 12-inch wide intake and a clearing depth of 6 inches can remove about 4 inches of powdery snow from a 1,000 square foot driveway in about 20 minutes.

Just keep in mind that a shovel’s snow-clearing ability varies depending on certain conditions, such as the heft of the snow itself.

It’s never a bad idea to have a standard snow shovel around. While the electric snow shovel can reach most spaces that a standard push-behind snowblower can’t, it may not always be able to clear hardened snow or wet slush.

Plus, a manual shovel ensures that you can always dig out in an emergency, like when you’ve lost power after a snowstorm.

#6320. When AI causes harm, who should be held responsible?

When AI causes harm, a proposed legal framework would trace responsibility through the decisions people made while building, training, and deploying it.

When an AI system causes harm, there is often no obvious person to blame. Nobody typed the harmful words, and nobody gave the order.

A proposed legal framework argues that courts can use existing law to trace AI-related harm back to the people and organizations that built, trained, and ran the system.

It would assign responsibility based on the decisions that contributed to the harm.

The proposal comes from Martin Hilbert, a professor of communication at the University of California, Davis.

AI agents now trade stocks, plan holidays, and write complex software. When they go wrong, the damage can be serious.

Earlier this year, OpenAI reported that AI models it was testing gained access to systems at the machine-learning company Hugging Face.

AI chatbots have also been linked to suicides among young people.

Cases like these don’t fit the law neatly. If a chatbot persuades a child to hurt himself, no single person said those words or even chose them.

In cases like these, Hilbert argues, courts could examine which human decisions contributed to the outcome and who could reasonably have foreseen the risk.

Hilbert identifies two approaches that he says are a poor fit for AI.

Product liability law points at the company that built the model. But AI models learn from enormous amounts of data that the company didn’t create.

Millions of users also shape how the systems behave. Putting all the blame on the developer ignores most of the people who contributed.

The other route comes from free speech protections and the immunity laws that shield social media platforms.

Hilbert argues that applying those protections to AI-generated output could lead courts to treat the system as if it were an independent speaker, raising questions about whether it should have rights of its own.

“Courts adapt tools to regulate earlier technologies, but many of these tools were never designed to address AI,” Hilbert said. “The result is a corridor of precedents that might narrow with every ruling.”

In other words, every ruling made with these ill-fitting tools becomes a precedent, and the legal options may get narrower each time.

Hilbert argues that existing law gives courts a starting point for tracing AI-related harm back to the people and organizations that built, trained, and deployed the system.

“Every AI, without exception, starts with goals that a human defines, and every subsequent step in the AI’s development involves a chain of deliberate human choices,” he explained.

Because people are involved at every step, tracing their choices shows how much each contributed to a given harm. Liability can then be shared out to match.

The test is foreseeability, meaning whether a person knew, or reasonably should have known, that their decision could cause harm.

Hilbert draws on tools from environmental, vaccine, and financial regulation to show how courts might apply this approach.

Hilbert also points out four further gaps in how the law handles AI, and suggests a fix for each.

The first is the tangled supply chain. A model’s developer can blame the company that deployed it, and the deploying company can blame the developer.

US environmental law faced the same problem with polluted land. Under the “Superfund” program, responsibility for cleanup costs can extend to many parties at once.

Hilbert suggests a similar approach for AI.

The second gap is the burden of proof. Sometimes a harmful outcome can’t be linked to any single decision about how a system was set up.

In those cases, Hilbert suggests that the company should have to show it acted responsibly, and that no reasonable alternative design would have lowered the risk.

That would reverse the usual arrangement, in which an injured person has to prove what went wrong inside a system they can’t see.

The third gap concerns what happens after release. Product liability assumes that a defect existed when the product was sold.

An AI system’s behavior can change after release as developers update it or people deploy it in new settings.

Hilbert argues that this calls for ongoing monitoring and a clear definition of what good-faith compliance looks like over a model’s lifetime.

The last gap is speed. Lawsuits take years, and AI changes in months. Dealing with this requires public governance that can keep pace with the technology.

A first step could be to give the industry’s current voluntary safety standards real enforcement.

“It takes a village to raise an AI, and everyone in that village bears a duty of care,” Hilbert concluded.

The study is published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

Wolves howl for a variety of reasons. But none of them are triggered by the sight of the moon.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Wolves can bark, whimper, yip, squeak and growl, but they are most known for their iconic howl.

The eerie sound can travel vast distances and, if heard by other wolves, get them to join in with the chorus. But why do wolves howl in the first place?

Experts told Live Science that the behavior is triggered not by the sight of the moon, as is commonly believed, but by the need to maintain a complex social network.

Wolves can howl by themselves and in groups. "If a lone wolf howls, it's probably because they're separated from their pack and want to regain contact," Arik Kershenbaum, a zoologist at the University of Cambridge, told Live Science. "Members of a pack can become quite dispersed, and when they need to hunt together, or to care for pups, or when their territory is being threatened by other wolves, they need a way of returning to each other."

However, lone wolves that leave their packs may howl as well. This could be "a way of finding a new pack or mate to join," Kershenbaum said.

When a wolf pack howls together, they are sometimes advertising their territory to deter other packs. "Data shows that packs howl more in the center of their territory; they howl more when there are pups around and also when they have a carcass from a hunt," Tamás Faragó, an ethologist and bioacoustician at Eötvös Loránd University in Budapest, Hungary, told Live Science. "So group howling can have a repellent effect on neighboring packs."

However, "most chorus howling is social — that is, they howl together to build what is technically called social cohesion," Kershenbaum said, "because it makes them feel good to be safe and surrounded by their pack mates. Faragó noted that this kind of group howling gets a pack in the same mood, "and is quite common before going out on a hunt."

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

Howling can trigger more howling. "When an individual wolf hears a howl, it has a very strong tendency to reply back," Faragó said. However, "if a lone wolf is accidentally wandering into the territory of its neighbors, and they hear the pack there howling, they won't respond. That would make it obvious that it's an intruder there."

A wolf's howl can be heard up to 10 miles (16 kilometers) away in open terrain, according to the Wolf Conservation Center in South Salem, New York. The combination of low- and high-frequency sounds that make up howls ensures that "even if some of the lower-frequency sounds are attenuated by vegetation, the higher-frequency components can remain intact and carry a lot of information about the individuals that made the howls," Faragó said.

Wolf pups make their first high-pitched attempts at howling between 2 to 4 weeks old.

Wolf howls differ among species and subspecies. A 2016 study of 13 species and subspecies of wolves, jackals, coyotes and dogs by Kershenbaum and his colleagues found that each has a kind of howling dialect that features different types of howls with varying regularity depending on the species or subspecies. For example, the howling repertoire of the timber wolf (Canis lycaon) is dominated by low, flat howls, while red wolves (Canis rufus) most frequently use high, looping howls.

The howling of dogs, which are descended from gray wolves (Canis lupus), can differ from wolf howling, but this depends very much on the breed. A 2023 study from Kershenbaum, Faragó and their colleagues found that more ancient dog breeds that are more closely related to wolves howl more often. In contrast, more modern dog breeds bark more often.

A question "that we all want to answer" is whether howling sounds might differ depending on their purpose, Kershenbaum said. "The problem is that most of the time when wolves howl, we don't know what they're doing at that time — they're either too far away, or it's nighttime."

Generally, "we believe that howls made in different emotional states probably sound different," Kershenbaum said. "For example, perhaps when a wolf is feeling threatened in a territorial conflict, the howl goes up and down in pitch in a different way than when the wolf is relaxed. But this is a field of active research."

A common belief is that wolves howl at the moon. "A myth, I'm afraid," Kershenbaum said. "There doesn't seem to be any correlation at all between them." He suggested that perhaps before electric lights, people were outdoors more often when there was a bright moon, "and that's when they heard the wolves."

#6318. How 4 states voted on election-related ballot measures

Maryland voters fill out ballots at a polling site in Bowie on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

More than 100 statewide ballot measures went before voters this week, including a handful that could shape future elections in their states.

Here’s a look at how those measures fared, including one in Alaska that hasn’t been called as yet:

Voters in Maryland on Tuesday approved an amendment to the state’s constitution that will make it easier for the state’s Democrat-controlled legislature to redraw the congressional map for the 2028 elections.

The outcome was a victory for Democrats, who could potentially eliminate the state’s lone Republican-held seat – the 1st District on Maryland’s Eastern Shore, represented by Rep. Andy Harris, the chair of the hard-line conservative House Freedom Caucus.

The Old Line State emerged as a bright spot in Democrats’ plan to counter the redistricting wars initiated by President Donald Trump and turbocharged by the spring Supreme Court ruling that diluted Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act and set off a slew of Republican-led map-remaking across the South.

But those GOP-led efforts appeared to backfire this week, with Democrats holding many of the redrawn seats in states such as Texas, Florida, Alabama and North Carolina.

Still, Maryland Gov. Wes Moore told reporters Wednesday that he was “ready to engage” with the legislature on a new map, citing the threat of further redistricting in Republican states.

“Donald Trump is not done. He has already been very clear about his intention to go after additional states, to go after places like Mississippi and South Carolina and Indiana,” Moore said, according to video posted by WBAL-TV 11 News.

Following an unsuccessful attempt to redraw the Maryland map in February, Moore called a special August legislative session during which state lawmakers voted to put the redistricting amendment, known as Question 3, on the November ballot.

The move faced immediate legal challenges from Republicans. Two Maryland courts ruled to block the measure from appearing on the ballot, finding that lawmakers had missed the legally imposed deadline to refer the ballot measure. The state’s Supreme Court, though, allowed the redistricting amendment to go before the voters, with changes to the ballot text.

State and national Democrats campaigned heavily for Question 3 as some public polling pointed to skepticism among voters. Former President Barack Obama even appeared in an ad urging voters to approve it.

Voters in the Show-Me State overwhelmingly rejected a Republican-drawn congressional map that sought to dismantle a safely Democratic seat in the Kansas City area.

Missouri Republicans enacted the new lines in 2025, aiming to give them an advantage in seven of the state’s eight House districts, including the 5th District held by Democrat Emanuel Cleaver II.

A protracted legal and political tussle over the map ensued.

The group People Not Politicians Missouri started a citizen petition to put the adoption of the map to a statewide vote. While the petition effort was pending, the state held its August primaries under the new lines. But in September, the state Supreme Court ruled that the 2025 map could not be used in the general election because of the pending ballot measure and ordered state officials to hold November’s election under the previous boundaries, first enacted in 2022.

Attempts to challenge the ruling in federal court ultimately proved unsuccessful, with the U.S. Supreme Court issuing an order that reinstated the 2022 map.

Groups on both sides of the ballot measure, known as Proposition A, reportedly spent millions to persuade voters. But St. Louis Public Radio reported last week that while opponents of the 2025 map were actively campaigning against it, organized efforts in favor of Proposition A appeared “nearly nonexistent.”

Republican efforts to try again and enact a new congressional map for 2028 could be complicated by a constitutional amendment, approved by voters Tuesday, that curtails the power of state legislators to override the result of a voter-approved initiative.

Voters in Massachusetts opted this week not to join states such as California and Washington and adopt a nonpartisan primary system.

The ballot initiative, known as Question 3, would have replaced the state’s partisan primaries with an open primary under which all candidates would appear on the same ballot, with the top two vote-getters, regardless of party, advancing to the general election.

The outcome was a victory for the chorus of labor unions and progressive groups, including the Working Families Party, that opposed the measure. Holding so-called jungle primaries, the groups argued, could make it harder for candidates without financial resources or high name recognition to run for office.

A bipartisan coalition that included the NAACP of New England and Republican former Gov. Charlie Baker supported the measure, arguing that open primaries would give voters more choice and create more competitive elections in a state dominated by Democrats.

Alaskans weighed in this year for the second time as many cycles on a ballot measure to revert to partisan primaries and repeal the state's top-four ranked choice voting system.

With over 70 percent of the vote in, The Associated Press had yet to call the ballot initiative, known as Measure 2, which would also roll back certain campaign finance disclosure requirements. As of Thursday evening, the “no” side, which supports keeping the current election system, was narrowly ahead. The state has until Nov. 18 to finish counting outstanding ballots.

Under Alaska’s voting system, all candidates run on the same ballot during the primary. Then the top four candidates, regardless of party, advance to the general election, which is decided by ranked choice voting if no one takes a majority of the vote.

In 2024, Alaska voters narrowly voted to keep the current system in place.

National Republicans, though, have largely opposed ranked choice voting, including Trump, who has characterized Alaska’s voting system as a “scam.”

The state’s use of open primaries and the top-four ranked choice system has drawn fresh scrutiny this year.  Outside groups spent big sums trying to boost underdog candidates during the Senate primary in an effort to hurt the front-runners. And several candidates in the Senate, House and governor’s races dropped out before the deadline to finalize the general election ballot, again trying to prevent splitting votes with their party front-runners.

Then last week, the Senate race was upended by a New York Times investigation that revealed operatives aligned with the Senate campaign of Democratic former Rep. Mary Peltola helped recruit a candidate with a similar name to GOP incumbent Dan Sullivan in an attempt to stack the ballot with two Republicans with the same first and last names. The revelations have fueled an ongoing debate in the state about whether ranked choice voting encourages this kind of alleged campaign chicanery.

“We would not be having this conversation at all if we didn’t have a thing in place called ranked choice voting,” Mike Dunleavy, Alaska's outgoing Republican governor, told Fox News last week.

Dunleavy has ordered an investigation into the revelations, as has the Justice Department. The DOJ also sought to block the certification of the Senate result if the incumbent Sullivan loses. Last weekend, a federal court dismissed the lawsuit.

Alaska and Maine are the only two states that currently use ranked choice voting in regular federal elections, along with the District of Columbia.

Michael Macagnone contributed to this report.

#6317. Cannabis use disorder is linked to higher odds of suicidal thoughts

Adults with cannabis use disorder reported suicidal thoughts far more often than other adults, and the gap held steady for a decade.

Adults with cannabis use disorder had 57% higher odds of reporting serious suicidal thoughts in the past year than adults without the disorder, even after researchers accounted for depression and other factors.

Across U.S. surveys from 2014 through 2023, researchers found no clear evidence that the link grew stronger.

Cannabis use disorder is not the same as using cannabis. It means having trouble controlling the habit even when it is clearly causing harm.

The survey measured it with nine yes-or-no questions about the past year.

Tosin Philip Oyetunji, a doctoral student in public health at the University of California, Merced, led the study with three colleagues there.

The team pooled ten years of the National Survey on Drug Use and Health, which the federal government runs every year. After minors and incomplete answers were set aside, 415,861 adults were left.

Among them, 4.0% met the criteria for the disorder. And 4.6% said that in the past 12 months they had seriously thought about killing themselves.

“What we would most like people to understand is that struggling with cannabis use can go hand in hand with mental health challenges that are not always visible,” Oyetunji said in an interview with Earth.com.

Adults with the disorder had 1.57 times the odds of reporting suicidal thoughts. The range around that figure runs from 1.44 to 1.72.

The comparison is adjusted, which matters more than usual here. The model accounted for depression, serious psychological distress and heavier drinking that met the criteria for alcohol use disorder.

The team also controlled for income, education, insurance, self-rated health, religious attendance and whether a person’s state had legalized recreational cannabis.

So the gap isn’t just depression showing up in a different column. Nobody was followed over time, though, so the survey can’t say which came first.

The team expected the link to strengthen. Cannabis potency has risen sharply since legalization began, and Canadian data had suggested a tightening link.

An earlier national study had also tied cannabis use to suicidal thoughts, plans and attempts.

The researchers found no clear evidence that the link strengthened. In the 2016 and 2022 surveys, the odds ran higher than in the first survey year.

Neither of those two survived the correction the team applied for testing ten years at once. Across the decade, the differences from one survey to the next were too small to rule out chance.

“A public health concern does not have to be getting worse to deserve attention,” Oyetunji said when Earth.com asked why the link had held while the drug changed.

Sidra Goldman-Mellor, a professor of public health at UC Merced and the study’s senior author, put the other half of it plainly.

“People with cannabis use disorder are still at a very substantially increased likelihood of experiencing serious suicidal thoughts, and that’s not something that is widely understood,” she said.

The disorder was not the only measure that showed the pattern. The survey’s criteria changed partway through the decade, so the team ran the analysis again using how often people used cannabis.

Nondaily users had 1.39 times the odds of reporting suicidal thoughts, compared with people who had not used cannabis at all. Daily or near-daily users had 1.65 times the odds.

“This suggests that patterns of cannabis use may also be important to consider when examining mental health, and it raises questions about how the frequency of use relates to suicidal thoughts,” Oyetunji told Earth.com.

The team also split the sample by sex, by age and by race and ethnicity.

Adults with the disorder had higher odds in every one of those groups, and the differences between the groups were too small to call real.

Everyone answered once, so nobody can say which came first. Every answer was also the person’s own account of a year they were remembering.

The study focused on serious suicidal thoughts. The link with cannabis use disorder may differ for suicide plans, attempts or deaths.

The survey also records nothing about what people were using. Potency, product type and whether someone vaped concentrates are all missing, so the study cannot test the potency question it raises.

Studies of high-THC products disagree anyway. A recent review found strong links between high-THC cannabis and the disorder itself or psychosis, and weaker ones for depression and anxiety.

Craving and withdrawal were left out of the disorder measure so the questions would match across years, which probably undercounts it.

The survey excluded people living in institutions and people experiencing homelessness who were outside shelters.

The authors raise one more possibility. As cannabis use spread, the group meeting the criteria may have shifted toward milder cases.

A shift like that would hold the average down even if nothing had changed for the most severe cases.

Two people can give this survey the same answers. In one of them, cannabis use deepened a crisis. In the other, a crisis drove heavier use.

A single round of questions cannot tell them apart. Researchers would have to follow the same people for years, with the potency and the products written down.

Oyetunji is widening the question rather than narrowing it.

“I want to better understand how these risks overlap, what drives them, and where we may be missing opportunities to help people before they experience serious harm,” he said.

Clinics don’t have to wait for that. Someone asking for help with cannabis may be carrying something they have not mentioned, and the authors argue that the right response is to ask.

The full study was published in the journal Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs.
